en: Commentary on the Vimalakīrti Sūtra, Scroll Three. Chapter Three: The Disciples.
Within this chapter, there is a brief analysis according to three sections: first, explaining the purpose of its inclusion; second, interpreting the chapter.
Third, explaining the meaning of the text.
To clarify the purpose of its composition:

However, the Sage’s profound penetration of the path of skillful means is non-dual; although the Layman manifested illness for the sake of sentient beings, the Tathāgata likewise harbored compassion and sent messengers to inquire after him.
Through this mutual exchange, the work of universal transformation, guidance, and benefit was extensively accomplished.
Therefore, this chapter follows.
Furthermore, as previously explained, the practice of prajñā and great compassion in conjunction with all virtues is termed "skillful means" (upāya).
This chapter specifically demonstrates that which transcends the cognitive capacity of those of the two vehicles and the various lesser bodhisattvas.
Now, this chapter is presented in order to manifest his superior virtues before him, so that he may abandon the inferior and cultivate the superior.
Alternatively, it may be said that within the preceding chapter, because of the inquiry regarding illness, the method for transforming ordinary beings was clarified.
Within this chapter, the illness of the noble ones is elucidated to clarify the transformative teaching of the noble Dharma.
Among the teachings for the noble ones, the śrāvakas are taught first;
therefore, this is this chapter.
Second, regarding the explanation of the names:
the Buddha, being endowed with supreme virtues, is called the Teacher of Gods and Humans;
those such as the śrāvakas who have personally received deliverance from the Buddha are called his disciples.
This is a designation derived from the relationship between teacher and disciple.
Furthermore, it is said that one who studies after the Buddha is called a "disciple" (di).
Those who are born through transformation from the Dharma are called "sons," and those whom he commands are his "disciples. Accordingly,
this chapter is titled the "Disciples Chapter" (Śrāvakavarga).
If one follows the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra*, it is called the "Chapter on Śrāvakas";
if one were to call it the "Chapter on Disciples," it might be confused with the "Bodhisattva" chapter.
Third, regarding the explanation of the textual meaning:
Within this passage, there is a threefold analysis:
first, an analysis distinguishing faults by way of characteristics;
second, an analysis by way of the beginning and end of the modes of practice.
Third, the explanation of the meaning according to the text.
First, regarding the manifestation of the loss of discrimination:
herein there are five hundred śrāvakas who practice.
These are the five hundred dharma-gates;
because they are abbreviated in this text, only ten are clarified.
These ten are precisely the dharmas attained by those who are śrāvakas.
Now, regarding the Mahāyāna, these are all instances of its failure; what are their characteristics?
First, Śāriputra was foremost among the śrāvakas in wisdom, yet because he did not penetrate the samādhi of eternal quiescence, [he failed].
For this reason, he was rebuked.
Second, Maudgalyāyana, who was foremost in supernatural powers,
was also rebuked because his teaching of the Dharma was improper, as his supernormal powers were not manifested before him.
The three Kāśyapas were foremost in the dhūta ascetic practices,
yet they were rebuked because their great compassion lacked impartiality.
Subhūti was foremost in understanding emptiness.
Because he had not attained the great emptiness of equality, he too was rebuked.
Fifth, Pūrṇa was foremost in eloquence;
because he did not penetrate the profound and far-reaching capacities of sentient beings, he too was rebuked.
Sixth, Kātyāyana was foremost in explaining the meaning of the teachings;
yet because he did not penetrate the profound meaning of true reality (*tattva-lakṣaṇa*), he too was rebuked.
Seventh, Aniruddha was foremost in the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*).
He was also rebuked because he did not practice in conjunction with signless wisdom (*animitta-prajñā*).
Upāli, who was foremost among those who uphold the Vinaya,
was also rebuked because he was unable to contemplate emptiness (*śūnyatā*) to extinguish his offenses.
The ninth, Upāli, was foremost in observing the precepts;
yet because he did not understand that there is no benefit in leaving the household life, he too was rebuked.
The tenth, Ānanda, was foremost in extensive learning.
Furthermore, because they do not understand the merits of the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body, they are also rebuked.
These ten points collectively manifest the failings of the disciples.
Second, regarding the analysis according to the beginning and end of the modes of practice:
First, Śāriputra practices the conduct of non-abiding.
Because this person has abandoned the secular world to return to the forest, eliminating distraction and attaining stillness,
he is now taught the practice of non-abiding in grasping or rejecting, thereby realizing the Middle Way.
This refers to the practice of non-abiding.
Second is Maudgalyāyana’s practice of entering and realizing through cultivation;
because Maudgalyāyana’s supernormal powers were not manifest, his teaching of the Dharma was inappropriate.
To teach the cultivation of the two kinds of emptiness and to realize the True Principle is called the practice of realization.
Mahākāśyapa and the other two Kāśyapas cultivated the practices that assist the Path.
Because these individuals have abandoned wealth for poverty and have not yet attained equanimity,
they are taught to cultivate the contemplation of equality to assist them in becoming Bodhisattvas;
this is called "conduct that aids the Path."
Fourth, Subhūti practices the cultivation of Great Emptiness (*mahāśūnyatā*).
Because he perceives through his auspicious insight that there are still notions of the heterodox and the orthodox, and has not yet realized true emptiness,
[the Buddha] instructs him to cultivate equanimous contemplation (*samadarśana*) so as not to grasp at the characteristics of the heterodox or the orthodox.
It is said that there are five types of great space-travelers (*ākāśa-gāmin*). Fifth is Pūrṇa, who practices the activity of preaching the Dharma;
however, because this person does not examine the faculties and desires [of his audience], he preaches the Dharma without adjusting it to their specific capacities.
He teaches by knowing the faculties and natures of beings, benefiting them universally according to what is appropriate for each;
this is called the practice of preaching the Dharma.
Sixth, Kātyāyana practiced the cultivation of understanding through birth.
Because these individuals extensively expound the five dharmas while deviating from their true characteristics,
teaching them to abandon the discriminating mind and to accord with practice that is signless,
it is called "the stage of generating understanding and practice."
The seventh, Aniruddha, cultivated the path of active application (*prāyogika*).
Because his divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) with signs (*sanimitta*) did not clearly perceive objects,
he was instructed to cultivate the signless divine eye (*animitta divyacakṣus*) to realize non-duality (*advaya*).
Yunqi said, "The Universal Practice (Sāmānyamārga) is for Upāli.

Because this person is unable to contemplate emptiness to extinguish offenses, he is taught to perform the signless repentance (animitta-pratikramaṇa), so that the defilements of offense do not arise."
This is called the cessation of unwholesome conduct.
Ninth, Rāhula cultivated the practice of renunciation;
because he was obscured by it, he did not realize that true renunciation is signless within signs.
He teaches the cultivation of the true renunciation that is free from marks and equal;
this is called the practice of renunciation.
Tenth, Ānanda, he cultivates the practice of the Dharma-body.
Because they do not yet fully understand that the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body is eternally abiding,
he teaches them to cultivate supramundane, unconditioned merit so as to forever leave behind the mind of arising and ceasing;
this is called the practice of the Dharma-body.
Third, regarding the explanation of the meaning of the text,
there are three distinct sections.
The first clarifies the intention behind Vimalakīrti’s feigning of illness, establishing it as the occasion for the arising of the questions.
Second, the Buddhas know [the situation] and inquire after the illness of Śrīgupta.
Third, from "In this way, the five hundred... onwards, it is a summary that categorizes and illustrates the preceding section.
At that time, Vimalakīrti thought to himself as he lay ill upon his bed: [text continues].
"At that time" refers to the moment when the thought arose.
"The elder Vimalakīrti" refers to the person who gave rise to the thought.
"He himself thought he was lying ill upon his bed" means that he was precisely generating this state of mind.
However, this thought was conceived because he waited for the Holy One’s inquiry; it was not that non-recollection constitutes a fault.
It is truly because Vimalakīrti’s compassion for sentient beings was so profound that he waited for the inquiry with the intensity of thirst, and thus gave rise to this thought.
Vimalakīrti manifested illness solely for the sake of sentient beings;
although his mind was directed toward them, the transformative work of attaining the influence and shadow of Buddhahood could only be accomplished through this means.
Thus, he considered himself to be lying ill upon his bed.
"Regarding 'yu' (于), it means 'at' (於).
'How could the World-Honored One, in his great compassion, not bestow pity?
means that the Buddha, possessing all virtues, is revered and sustained by the world."
Therefore, he is called the World-Honored One (*Bhagavān*).
He is the pinnacle of compassion, such that none can surpass him;
since his actions accord with principle and bring fulfillment, how could he not be "Great"?
"Neiṅ" (寧) means "capable";
"mǐn" (慜) means "to pity.
Vimalakīrti spoke of himself thus.
"My young son’s compassion is still deficient; he remains entangled by afflictions.
How much more so for the Buddha, a person of supreme excellence—how could he not show pity and send inquiries?
Knowing his intention, the Buddha immediately addressed him. This concludes the second section: the inquiry regarding illness concerning Right Livelihood (*samyagājīva*).
Because the timing was opportune and it was destined to take place here, he was sent to inquire and could not be stopped.
Nevertheless, according to the main thrust of the text, there are roughly three reasons why the others were dismissed while the primary messenger was directed toward Mañjuśrī.
First, it was announced publicly to demonstrate that the Tathāgata’s mind is impartial and without bias;
this is similar to how he addressed the great assembly together in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* to allow for questions.
Second, it was necessary to announce it publicly because he wished to extensively entrust these words to the multitude to manifest the supreme virtue of Vimalakīrti.

The command given to those incapable of manifesting his virtue was to announce that he was incapable; the command given to those capable of manifesting his sublime virtue was to reveal its excellence.
Thirdly, because he wished to extensively entrust these words to a multitude of voices in order to manifest the Dharma taught by Vimalakīrti, it was necessary to issue a general announcement.

Therefore, in the subsequent text, those who are unfit are first addressed to clarify what was taught in the past, while those who are fit are subsequently addressed to elucidate what is being taught now.
Thus, among the disciples to whom this general announcement is made, there are ten distinct types of individuals.
As for the reason Śāriputra was summoned first:

it was because he was an unsurpassed messenger and not one who could be dispatched by anyone other than a man of great penetration; for Śāriputra’s divine wisdom was transcendent and peerless, and thus he was summoned first.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
Within the city of Rājagṛha, there was a great master of treatises named King Mādhara.
Because of his intelligence, the king bestowed upon him the governance of an entire district as a reward.
She gave birth to a daughter whose eyes resembled those of a śāri bird;
she was named accordingly.
He was also named Śāriputra,
receiving his title from the śārikā bird.
At that time, there was a great master of treatises in the kingdom of South India.
He was named Upatiṣya. Carrying a brazier upon his head—
fearing that the copper leaves of his belly, which were ignorant and darkened by worldly things, might overflow with the poetry and scriptures—
he struck the drum of debate.
The people of the country all gathered together, wishing to determine who was superior and who was inferior.
On the road, Madhura saw two fighting bulls and knew that his opponent would defeat him.
Thereupon, he entered the assembly to engage in debate, but he immediately fell into a position of defeat.
The ministers deliberated together to seize his fiefdom in order to bestow it as a reward upon Tiṣya. Māthara said to Tiṣya,
"The King has granted you a fief as a reward because of your intelligence."
I took her as my wife. Later,
while she was pregnant, she suddenly saw a man in a dream during the night.
Clad in armor and holding a vajra in her hand, she shattered all the mountains;
thereafter, she stood at the edge of one mountain.
Having awakened, she immediately spoke to her husband.
Her husband explained,
"You shall become pregnant;
the child you carry will certainly be a son."
"One whose body has shattered armor must be a child of profound virtue;
one who holds a vajra in hand [is likewise so]."
"This child is intelligent and possesses great wisdom.
As for his name, 'Destroyer of All Mountains,' he shall become a great master of treatises who refutes all proponents of other doctrines."
Then, as he stood by the side of a mountain,
he should subdue one person to serve as his disciple;
for since the time she first conceived, his mother’s spiritual wisdom has been extraordinary.
In the past, when she debated with her elder brother on points of doctrine, he always emerged victorious;
however, once his sister became pregnant, her brother’s arguments were defeated.
From this, it was known that the child’s wisdom would benefit his mother’s own intelligence.
At the age of seven, he was the foremost in debating within the sixteen great kingdoms.
He left the household life as a disciple of the Buddha and became the foremost among the disciples in wisdom.
Therefore, in other sūtras and śāstras, Śāriputra is praised as follows:
except for the wisdom and erudition of the Buddha-Tathāgata, the wisdom and erudition of all classes of sentient beings cannot equal even one-sixteenth part of that of Śāriputra.
He then informed him first.
Why did he inform him first?
Because his generosity was superior, he informed him first for that reason.
Question: It was previously stated that the Buddha spoke first because the voice’s virtue was inferior;
yet Śāriputra is the most eminent among the disciples. Why is this?
Why was he informed first?
The explanation says:
although Śāriputra’s wisdom and conduct were superior, his other practices were inferior to those of others.
Therefore, he was able to inform [the Buddha] beforehand. If this were the case,
then among the remaining nine persons, there would be distinctions of superior and inferior virtue.
One should also first inform [them].
If one were to argue according to this logic, it would be untenable;
rather, the Great Sage employs various skillful means to guide others, informing them whenever it is appropriate to do so.
How could there be a sequence of before and after?
Within this passage, there are four parts.
First, the command to inquire after his illness.
First, the refusal; second, the inability to comply;
third, the explanation of the reason;
fourth, the conclusion of the inability to comply.
The subsequent passages are analogous.
The first command may be understood.
Regarding the second, the refusal on the grounds of inability:
He recounted all his past humiliations to demonstrate that he was unable to endure them;
it was not that he harbored such thoughts because of this particular shame.
Nevertheless, the Buddha is a Great Being whose words are like a seal and cannot be contravened.
Why is it that those who deliver messages act merely as the Buddha’s envoys?
They must be men of realization;
recall how in the past, when rebuked, they were unable to respond because they remained silent.
Now, fearing such a loss and apprehensive that there might be the disgrace of bringing shame upon your honor,
I have sent these subordinates to offer their formal words of farewell.
In the third explanation, there are two distinct points of meaning:
first, the account of the events of his previous rebuke;
second, from the passage beginning "At that time, Vimalakīrti... onwards, the clarification of the characteristics of the instruction and rebuke regarding gain and loss.
He censures their faults and instructs them to cultivate virtue.

Within the preceding section, the phrase "Why is this so? serves as a general self-interrogation. If one considers the intent behind the World-Honored One’s command for those to inquire after his illness, it is as follows:
[The text continues: ...If one were to act according to the World-Honored One’s intention in commanding these inquiries, [then...]
"You are my disciple; I have sent you to inquire after his illness. Why did you not go? This inquiry serves as a self-examination.
In the following examples, there are always two intended meanings.
From "Recalling [the past]" onwards, the text explicitly sets forth the matter of the reprimand.

Those who have previously sat in meditative seclusion beneath trees in the forest—such as the Śrāvakas practicing concentration—must rely on external conditions of stillness; they do not know that tranquil concentration is free from all conditions.
Thus, although Śāriputra had attained Arhatship, his attachment to dharmas (dharmagrāha) was not yet extinguished.
Seeing that the body and mind were afflicted by the suffering of physical toil and vexation, he wished to conceal his form within the forest;
seeing that the mind was agitated and distracted, he further wished to hide the mind within meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
This was because the grasping and rejecting of body and mind had not yet been harmonized.
The reason for being rebuked is truly due to not yet having realized the emptiness of dharmas,
whereby one perceives the external six sense-objects as that which disturbs.
Because they perceive the six internal sense-faculties as being disturbed,
they rely on forests to attain stillness and avoid external defilements.
"To rest" (yan) means to be silent.
Because one sits silently beneath a tree with a settled mind in meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), it is called "seated in repose" (*yànzuò*).
The second section, concerning the meaning of the instruction to reprove, is divided into three parts.
First, the reproach.
The second is the teaching and the third is the interrogation;
it is not necessarily sitting that constitutes "sitting in meditation"— this was a rebuke of his error.
There are six kinds of "losses," which, when reversed according to the text of the lower teaching, become the six virtues.
Because Śāriputra attained the state of physical and mental integration while sitting in meditation under a tree, he concealed his body in the forest and hid his mind in meditative absorption.
Although one wishes to conceal it, it instead becomes manifest.
Since this is not entirely incorrect, it is said that "it need not arise" rather than saying it is "not. This means that while it need not be so, it is not stated to be non-existent.
Thus, it is simply that it need not be so, but it is not said to be non-existent.
The method of sitting for the two vehicles may indeed be embodied [in practice];
however, it is not necessarily so, for it is not the ultimate, true method of sitting of the Mahāyāna.
Zhuangzi said:
It must be that he dwells with attachment while sitting.
Śāriputra perceives that there is distraction which can be discerned and tranquility which can be rejoiced in;
therefore, [the Buddha] now rebukes him, saying that it is not necessary for sitting to constitute "sitting in meditation" (yañ-sa).
If one explains the arising of the *śarīra* in terms of practice, it refers to those who do not abide in conditioned activity;
for such persons have abandoned the secular world to return to the forest for the sake of tranquil concentration,
and are now taught not to abide in grasping or rejecting.
This constitutes the Great Samādhi.
The section beginning with "Not manifesting body or mind within the three realms" marks the second reversal, which clarifies the correct teaching after having dispelled errors.
There are six aspects of this teaching.
First, by breaking through both body and mind, one destroys the marks of body and mind.
Second, by concentrating and stilling the mind, one breaks through and destroys the grasping at the marks of stillness and agitation.
Third, by merging the ultimate and the conventional, one breaks through and destroys the grasping at the marks of ordinary and holy beings.
Fourth, by extinguishing both internal and external, one destroys the grasping at the characteristics of internal and external.
Fifth, by merging the heterodox and the orthodox, one destroys the grasping at the characteristics of heterodoxy and orthodoxy.
Sixth, by equalizing bondage and liberation, one destroys the grasping at the characteristics of bondage and liberation.
Regarding the statement that "in the former and middle [turnings], he did not manifest body or mind within the three realms," this refers to the body and mind of the first [turning] and so forth.
Yuan (Yuǎn) says:
The realms of desire, form, and formlessness constitute the three realms.
Ordinary beings receive the fruit of physical form within both the realms of desire and form, which is termed the "manifest body.
Within the realm of formlessness, they receive the fruit of mind and mental factors, which is termed the "manifest mind."
The Bodhisattva realizes that the three realms are illusory and are merely the products of the mind; having realized this, they abandon them, finding no place where they can exist.
Therefore, they do not manifest body or mind within the stages of the three realms.
This is what constitutes sitting in meditative repose. Pūrṇa said:
"The śrāvakas attain the characteristics of body and mind."
Therefore, although he concealed his body within the forest and hid his mind in meditative absorption,
his very desire to remain hidden resulted instead in his being manifest.
The Great Being realized that the nature of the bodies and minds within the three realms is fundamentally empty.
Not grasping, not abandoning, and not manifesting body or mind—
this is called "sitting in meditation.
It is also said:
Because the five faculties are empty, the mind does not manifest.
That the nature of body and mind is empty is true seated meditation.
Sengzhao said:
"The Dharma-body sits in tranquil repose; both form and spirit are extinguished.
The Way transcends ordinary realms and is beyond the reach of sight and hearing."
How could he still manifest his body within the triple world to cultivate the mind for the sake of meditative concentration?
Although Śāriputra still possessed a physical body born of worldly retribution and its associated marks,
because he regarded the human realm as a source of disturbance, he concealed his body in the forest and withdrew his mind into meditative absorption.
Though one may wish to conceal oneself in order to manifest,
one cannot yet achieve the state where form and spirit leave no trace and both grasping and rejecting have perished.
How could one run down a long road to avoid one's shadow, or heat flowing water in search of ice?
The reason for this reprimand is precisely because of this:
one who manifests majestic deportment while remaining in the meditative absorption of non-arising and non-extinction commits the second fault of agitation within stillness.
Those of the two vehicles suffer from mental toil and anxiety;
when they temporarily suspend their mental conceptions, it is called the "extinction samādhi.
Because the fundamental consciousness (ālayavijñāna) sustains the physical body, it does not perish.
Because the six consciousnesses have ceased, they cannot initiate movement.
This is because the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) that gives rise to the deportment of a Śrāvaka has been eliminated.
When entering the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti), the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) ceases;
therefore, one enters this absorption by relinquishing it during the four postures (īryāpatha).
It is not so for a Bodhisattva.
It is quiescent yet constantly active;
stillness and turbulence are no different. Why is this so?
Because they are without mind, they do not arise from the meditative absorption of cessation;
yet, with a mindless mind, they manifest dignified deportment.
It is like a wish-fulfilling jewel that, without mental discrimination, naturally rains down all manner of precious objects.
It can only be realized through spiritual intuition;
it is difficult to seek through mundane affairs.
To come and go without duality is what constitutes "sitting in repose."
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: Puṣpa said,
"Do you believe and accept that all dharmas possess the characteristic of eternal quiescence?"
Śāriputra said, "I believe this.
Samantakusuma said:
All phenomena are eternally quiescent and lack intrinsic substance.
Alternatively, it may be that when a Bodhisattva enters the meditative absorption of cessation,
although the six consciousnesses are absent, the wisdom of equality remains.
It gives rise to the physical body capable of manifesting dignified deportment (*īryāpatha*).
The meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) of the Two Vehicles lacks the Wisdom of Equality (*samatājñāna*), and thus cannot manifest such deportment. Zhaò said:
When those of the Lesser Vehicle enter meditative absorption, their forms become like withered trees, devoid of any capacity for movement or function.
When a Bodhisattva enters the samādhi of ultimate reality (*bhūtatathatā*),
their mental and cognitive faculties are eternally quiescent, yet their physical form pervades the eight directions.
Transforming in accordance with capacities and responding to occasions without fixed method;
in every movement and pause, never abandoning dignified decorum—
this is true seated meditation.
Regarding "not abandoning the principle of the path-dharma while attending to the affairs of ordinary beings," the third [point] is the integration of the ultimate and the conventional. Yuan says:
Precepts, meditative concentration, wisdom, and so forth are the dharmas of the noble path;
greed, anger, ignorance, and so forth are mundane phenomena.
The followers of the Hīnayāna have not yet realized the emptiness of dharmas.
One perceives that there may be karma that exists and is fearsome;
having already entered the noble state, one is unable to manifest it in order to guide sentient beings.
The Bodhisattva thoroughly understands emptiness while knowing existence;
dwelling amidst illusions, they are without fear and manifest their conduct for the sake of teaching and transforming others.
That defilement and purity are non-dual is what constitutes sitting in meditation.
Furthermore, because the Great Being possesses fundamental wisdom, he constantly contemplates true suchness.
This is called "not abandoning the dharmas of the Path.
Within the wisdom attained subsequently (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), one harmonizes with all things like light;
to transform sentient beings, one manifests as an ordinary person.
It is further said:
"In the wisdom attained after meditation (prsthalabdha-jñāna), the mind is constantly in a state of meditative absorption, never abandoning the dharmas of the Path;
yet within the mind of great compassion (mahākaruṇā), afflictions manifest in order to teach and transform sentient beings."
Therefore, it is said that he manifests the affairs of ordinary beings. Manzhu says:
"Śrāvakas are unable to immediately purify what is defiled."
Obstructed by birth and death, one cannot remain in the middle to transform sentient beings.
The Great Being (mahāsattva), however, brings both good and evil to rest and contemplates both the ultimate and the conventional simultaneously;
thus, they can abide in the Middle Way while manifesting the affairs of ordinary people.
Therefore, the subsequent scripture states:
"Manifesting the experience of the five desires to clearly demonstrate the affairs of ordinary beings, yet also manifesting the practice of dhyāna,
is called not abandoning the dharmas of the Path."
These are words concerning the function of transformation.
In reality, the Great Being does not perceive any dharma of the Path as being distinct from ordinary phenomena;
they are of one mark, signless, equal, and without differentiation.
Regarding "the mind does not abide within nor does it abide without":
the fourth [category] is the internal and external.
The six sense faculties are the internal.
The six sense objects are external.
For a śrāvaka, when entering meditative concentration, the mind is internal;
upon emerging, it is external.
When internal and external are not yet equalized, the essence is not fixed.
The Bodhisattva realizes that both internal and external are fundamentally empty; as characteristics arise, they are not existent, and thus internal and external are equal.
This is what constitutes sitting in meditative repose.
Therefore, the sutra below says:
"Without dwelling on internal or external [phenomena], one practices equanimity."
Alternatively, it may be that the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) is internal and the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) is external.
The followers of the Two Vehicles cling to the existence of these truths and thus their minds wander between the internal and external;
whereas Bodhisattvas realize that both the ultimate and the conventional are empty, and therefore do not dwell within or without.
It is further said:
that which depends on others (paratantra) is internal,
while the imagined nature (parikalpita) is external.
The followers of the Lesser Vehicle do not realize that both the grasper and the grasped are empty; they wander within and without.
The Great Beings know that the nature of both the internal and external is empty, and for this reason, they do not abide in either the internal or the external.
Regarding "practicing the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment while remaining unmoved by any views," the fifth [point] is the merging of the heterodox and the orthodox.
Yuan says:
The five views are not one, and thus they are called "the various views":

the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), adherence to rules and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), and adherence to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*).
Ordinary persons constantly give rise to these and are unable to enter into correctness.
The practitioners of the Two Vehicles cannot enter into error because they cultivate what is correct;
the Bodhisattva, however, manifests conduct for the sake of teaching and transforming sentient beings, and thus remains unmoved.
Although he manifests as being identical to those in error, his inner mind is constantly correct, equanimous, and impartial.
This is what constitutes sitting in meditative repose.
Therefore, the subsequent scripture states:
"There are eighty-four thousand gateways of affliction, through which all sentient beings become exhausted."
The Buddhas perform the work of a Buddha precisely through this Dharma.
Sengzhao says:
"The Hinayana cannot transform the heterodox into the orthodox."
One must necessarily sever [wrong] views through the path of cultivation.
When a Mahāsattva thoroughly penetrates all views,
they are no different from the factors of enlightenment.
Therefore, one does not depart from insight while practicing the factors of enlightenment.
Thus, the subsequent sutra states:
"One who abides in the right path does not discriminate between the false and the correct."
It is also said:
"Ordinary beings are mired in existence;
those of the Two Vehicles delight in emptiness."
The various views act as fetters;
only by relinquishing them can one be liberated.

Furthermore, there is no characteristic of a grasping subject that can take an object as its focus.
Therefore, Vimalakīrti said:
"Dharmas are without grasping because they have no focal object."
In the two subsequent phrases, the first phrase refutes names and refutes discourse;
the second phrase refutes the mental cognition that departs [from them], thereby establishing the aforementioned detachment from discourse.
Regarding the first phrase, "dharmas have no names":
Yuan says: This precisely clarifies that there is no [inherent] principle.
That is to say, within the true Dharma, there are no names, words, or phrases established by deluded conceptualization.
By destroying verbal expression, one reveals and establishes the nameless.
Since names are the basis of speech,
because there is no name, language does not arise.
Therefore, it is called a "segment of speech.
To claim that by citing a segment of speech one establishes non-existence is not a correct interpretation.
What is called the "root of speech"?
It can only be said to be the root of names;
language is the root of names.
Ultimate reality is profoundly deep and transcends words;
how could it possess names?
Of phenomena, there is no speaker.
This clearly demonstrates that principle is non-existent;
within the true Dharma, speech does not arise,
and therefore there is no verbal expression.
That which is free from applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*) destroys emotional attachment to reveal the principle;
applied and sustained thought are the causes of verbal expression.
Because within the true Dharma there is no vitarka (applied thought) or vicāra (sustained thought), speech does not arise;
therefore, there is no verbal expression.
Gross thinking is termed vitarka.
"Careful reflection is called contemplation (vitarka).
These are all conceptual appearances;
because the true Dharma transcends conceptualization, it is without applied thought (vitarka) or sustained thought (vicāra)."
Question:
In the first dhyāna there is both vitarka (applied thought) and vicāra (sustained thought);
in the intermediate dhyāna there is no vitarka but there is vicāra.
From the second dhyāna upward, there is neither vitarka nor vicāra.
What difference is there between this and the true Dharma, which is free from vitarka and vicāra? Answer:
The true nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is extinguished because it is fundamentally non-arising;
therefore, it is said to be "non-existent.
From the second dhyāna upward, because one transcends the antidotes [of the lower stages], it is called "separation from vitarka and vicāra."
That "dharmas are formless" correctly explains that there is no principle [of form].
This means that within the true dharma, there are no aggregates (*skandha*) or formal characteristics (*nimitta*).
By this, he concludes the preceding meaning of being free from characteristics.
Therefore, it is said to be signless (*animitta*).
It is illustrated by analogy with space:
because the true Dharma is free from signs, just like worldly space, it is said to be "like space."
The statement that "dharmas are without conceptual proliferation" (aprapañca) precisely clarifies that there is no [intrinsic] principle [to be grasped].
All names and expressions outside of this principle constitute conceptual proliferation;
because the true dharma is free from these, it is said to be without conceptual proliferation.
By this, the meaning of the previously mentioned "separation from names" is concluded;
therefore, it is said that there is no conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). The term "ultimate emptiness" (*atyanta-śūnyatā*) is explained as a manifestation of non-existence.
The principle that transcends all verbal discourse is called ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*).
Above, we have clarified that phenomena are devoid of characteristics by way of the aggregates (*skandha*);
hereafter, secondly, we shall clarify that phenomena are devoid of characteristics by way of the eighteen elements (*dhātu*).
The text consists of nineteen sentences,
which are divided into two sections in meaning.
The first section, consisting of one sentence, clarifies the non-self of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*).
The subsequent eighteen phrases clarify the non-self of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*).
Regarding the first phrase:
"That which is the non-self of phenomena" correctly demonstrates the absence of intrinsic principle.
This means that within the true Dharma there is no self (*ātman*) nor anything belonging to a self (*ātmīya*).
The meaning is as explained above.
Because it is free from "what belongs to a self," this is used to clarify its non-existence.
Regarding the eighteen phrases concerning the emptiness of the lower dharmas, they are grouped into three sections.
The first section consists of six phrases,
which clarify the emptiness of the six sense faculties.
The six lines beginning with "Dharmas are immovable" clarify the emptiness of the six consciousnesses.
The seven lines beginning with "Dharmas are free from the beautiful and the ugly" clarify the emptiness of the six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*).
Within the first six lines:
The first three [sections] refute appearances, while the latter three establish reality.
Within the first three,
the initial phrase clarifies that the sense faculties are empty by way of consciousness.
The second [section] clarifies the emptiness of the sense faculties by reference to their objects;
the third reveals the emptiness of the sense faculties by reference to their causes.
Regarding the first sentence:
Regarding the non-differentiation of phenomena (*dharma*), it correctly establishes that there is no principle [of differentiation].
Within true phenomena (*dharmatā*), the six sense faculties do not exist;
the arising of consciousness that cognizes objects is termed "non-differentiation."
The phrase "because it is free from all consciousnesses" explains this by revealing its non-existence.
While consciousness arises within the six sense faculties according to the boundaries of objective phenomena,
within the true Dharma, such consciousness does not exist.
Therefore, it is called "detached from all consciousnesses.
Because it is detached from all consciousnesses, there is no conceptual discrimination.
Furthermore, it says:
Regarding "non-conceptualization":
within the true Dharma, there are no three kinds of conceptualization.
The first is conceptualization of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-vikalpa*).
The second is recollective discrimination (*anusmaraṇa-vikalpa*).
The third is calculating discrimination (*abhinirūpaṇā-vikalpa*).
As for intrinsic discrimination (*svabhāva-vikalpa*):
This refers to the discrimination of the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) as they are perceived in the present;
and the discrimination of recollection (*anusmaraṇa-vikalpa*), which refers to the discrimination that pursues and recalls conditioned phenomena previously experienced.
This refers to the conceptualization that forcibly constructs and discriminates regarding the past, future, and present when they are not manifest.
Among the eight consciousnesses, only the sixth mental consciousness possesses all three types of discrimination;
the remaining seven consciousnesses possess only the discrimination of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-vikalpa*).
Because it takes the present as its object,
or perhaps the seventh manas-consciousness also possesses investigative discrimination (*abhinirūpaṇā-vikalpa*),
since it investigates and clings to a self.
As for its essential nature,
according to the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra*,
the conceptualizing discrimination (*abhinirūpaṇā-vikalpa*) has wisdom (*prajñā*) as its essence.
Recollection and conceptualization have mindfulness as their nature;
discrimination has cognition as its nature.
Within the true Dharma, there are neither delusions nor the eight consciousnesses.
Therefore, there is no such discrimination. That phenomena have no "comparison" (pramāṇa) means that, when correctly analyzed, their intrinsic nature is non-existent.
When characteristics and sense-objects confront one another, this is termed "comparison."
The true Dharma has no such designation; it is incomparable.
It is explained as "without dependence" to reveal its non-existence.
Because it lacks roots and objects that could mutually depend upon one another, it is said to be "without dependence."
Perhaps there might be a comparison between existence and non-existence;
however, since all phenomena lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), how could they depend on anything? Therefore, [the text] reveals their non-existence.
Since existence does not exist, what could non-existence possibly be?
Because both existence and non-existence are empty, they do not depend upon one another.
It is like the ring finger:
that which is long in form is considered short when compared to a shorter finger, while that which is short is considered long when compared to a longer one.
The nature is neither long nor short.
Thus, the essential nature of the true Dharma is inherently empty; being devoid of the natures of existence and non-existence, it is free from mutual dependence.
Therefore, the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states:
"If a phenomenon is established in dependence upon causes,
that very establishment depends [upon those causes]."
Now, there is neither dependence on causes nor any dharma that is produced.
A dharma does not belong to its cause.
This clearly demonstrates that while there is no [intrinsic] principle [of causality], in terms of the delimitation of phenomena, the fruit arises from the cause;
because the cause subsumes the fruit, it is said to "belong to" the cause.
The true Dharma lacks this designation because it does not belong to causes and does not reside in conditions;
thus, it is explained as "non-existent" to reveal its absence.
That which produces [an effect] directly is called a cause.
That which is distant yet assists in its manifestation is called a "condition" (pratyaya),
just as in the case of conventional dharmas,
where the seed is the causal ground (hetu) and water is the condition.
When sprouts and fruits are able to arise,
and conditions exist,
one may then speak of their belonging to causes in relation to them.
There can be no object [of cognition] present.
Knowing this, to whom could one possibly address the statement that it "belongs to a cause"?
Or perhaps it is so.
"Condition" (*pratyaya*) is another designation for "cause" (*hetu*).
To say that [the Tathāgata] does not exist within conditions should be understood as meaning that he does not exist within causes.
One cannot speak of it again to clarify that it does not abide within conditions.
Birth is inseparable from conditions, and thus it is termed "abiding";
the Truth (the Real) does not rely upon conditions, and therefore it is said not to abide within conditions.
Therefore, it does not belong to causes.

From the following three phrases, the identity with reality (*tattva*) is revealed by means of the three meanings of *tathatā* (suchness), *dharmatā* (dharma-nature), and *bhūtakoṭi* (the limit of reality).
How do these three differ?
Within the true Dharma, emptiness is called "suchness" (tathatā); that which has a name is called the "dharma-nature" (dharmatā).
That which is neither existent nor non-existent is described as the "reality limit" (bhūtakoṭi) and the "truth" (satya).
What is emptiness? It is the absence of characteristics and the absence of intrinsic nature. What is non-emptiness?
Because it is endowed with the Buddha-dharmas.
The *Śraddhotpāda Śāstra* states:
"First, true emptiness reveals the essence of the Dharma."
Because emptiness is not false;
second, it is non-empty according to reality.
Next, the essence of the Dharma is revealed.
Because it is fully endowed with the qualities of the untainted nature (*anāsrava-dharma*).
Why, then, is it called neither existent nor non-existent?
Existence and non-existence are of one essence, abiding in reality (*tattva*).
It is further stated:
"Dharmatā, True Suchness (Tathatā), and the Limit of Reality (Bhūtakoṭi)—these three are all alternative names for the true mark (lakṣaṇa).
They are named as such because they accord with reality and are unchanging."
Thus, the cause of all these phenomena is called the "dharma-nature" (dharmatā).
Reaching its ultimate limit is termed the "limit of reality" (bhūtakoṭi).
Regarding the statement that from the beginning through the middle, phenomena are identical to the dharma-nature:
I shall now provide a correct exposition.
Within the Tathāgatagarbha, all Buddha-dharmas are termed "dharma-nature" (dharmatā).
The true dharma being expounded here is of one essence with that.
Because it is one and not different, it is said to be "identical.
The phrase "because it enters into all phenomena" is explained to reveal this identity;
"enters" (ru) here means "to accord with" (shun).
Because they accord with all dharmas, they share a single nature.
These dharmas are precisely the dharmas of untainted (anāsrava) qualities;
they are not the dharmas of the five aggregates (pañcaskandha).
Therefore, Vimalakīrti said:
"Because phenomena are identical to the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) and enter the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu).
Question:
Since the essence of the Dharma is one,
how can it be called "conforming" or "entering"? Answer:
Although their essential nature is one, the gates of meaning are always distinct; though the meanings differ, their substance is the same.
Thus they are said to "accord with and enter" [the truth].
The following cases are all likewise so.
Regarding the phrase "the Dharma conforms to suchness" (yathābhūta),
Yuǎn says: it means that when the characteristics [of phenomena] are correctly discerned, they are not different from the meaning of true suchness (tathatā).
Although the dharma-realm is distinct,
the principle of emptiness is no different;
therefore, it is described as "suchness."
The Dharma being analyzed accords with that [reality] in accordance with reason; therefore, it is called "conforming" (anuvartin).
Since this is identical to the One, for what reason is it called "conforming"?
The meaning is as explained previously.
Because the gates are distinct while their substance is the same, one may speak of them as "conforming.
The previous case is the same as this one.
"Following words" means they are merely on the ears.
"Having nothing to follow" explains and establishes the meaning of "following," because there is nothing to follow within existent phenomena (*dharmas*).
Therefore, it conforms to suchness. This may be so;
for it does not merely conform to existence.
Nor does it follow non-existence;
because it is free from both existence and non-existence, it accords with suchness (*tathatā*).
It is further said:
If there were dharmas existing externally, then there would be something to follow;
however, all things are like that which has nothing to follow.
One who abides in the reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi) should correctly discern the characteristics [of phenomena].
"Limit" (*koṭi*) is a synonym for a boundary or extremity.
The point of ultimate exhaustion is called the "limit of reality" (*bhūtakoṭi*).
The true dharma that has been analyzed is said to "abide" within this limit of reality.
The preceding passage, "abiding in accordance with this," likewise refers to both the left and right.
The phrase "immovable on all sides" establishes the meaning of abiding:
because one is not swayed by the two extremes of existence and non-existence, one abides in the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"The *prajñāpāramitā* is like a great mass of fire that cannot be touched from any of its four sides;
it is far removed from the four positions (*catuskoṭi*)."
Tán said: "In reality, to have the false outside [of the real] is precisely to have limits and to be subject to movement.
Since the false is eternally the True, there are no limits and nothing that can move."
The five subsequent lines clarify consciousness within emptiness:
the first two refute characteristics,
while the latter three reveal reality.
In the first two lines, the first line clarifies the emptiness of consciousness by reference to objects,
while the second line clarifies emptiness directly with respect to the substance of consciousness itself.
Regarding the phrase "dharmas are without movement" in the first line:
This clearly explains that in principle there is no [movement].
The mind of the six consciousnesses goes and comes to grasp sensory objects; this is called "agitation.
True Dharma is eternally abiding and is not like that; thus it is called "non-agitation."
"Not relying on the six sense objects" means that by analogy it is revealed as non-existent;
because it does not arise in dependence upon the six sense objects like the six consciousnesses, it is without movement or fluctuation.
It may be so. When false consciousness grasps objects as external realms, it stirs the mind; this is called "agitation.
True Mind is free from thought; although it conditions myriad phenomena, because its conditioning is without an object of condition, it is without agitation.
"Phenomena have no going or coming" correctly clarifies that there is no [substantial] principle [of movement].
The mind of the six consciousnesses, which transmigrates through the three periods of time, is what is termed "going and coming."
"Going" refers to the past;
"coming" refers to the future.
Since the true Dharma is detached from these, it has neither going nor coming.
"Never abiding" is explained as a manifestation of non-existence;
the present is called "abiding."
If a real dharma were to have previously existed in the present, one could speak of its "going" or "coming" in relation to it;
however, since no dharma exists in the present,
with respect to what could one speak of "coming" or "going"?
These two involve the elimination of characteristics; the latter three are the reality itself.
"Dharma conforming to emptiness" refers to the gate of emptiness;
"conforming to signlessness" refers to the gate of signlessness.
This should be understood through the gate of non-action and non-acting.
According to the *Madhyāntavibhāga*,
emptiness is of three kinds.
First is the emptiness of non-existence,
which refers to the fact that the nature of conceptual construction is entirely without substance.
Second is the emptiness of being unreal.

That is to say, the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), being dependently originated and unreal, is not the same as the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), which is absolutely non-existent.
This is the emptiness of the three natures.

That is to say, the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*)—namely, the absence of marks and the absence of arising in the aforementioned two natures—is the emptiness of self-nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*).
The signless also has three aspects:
first, the absence of the mark of a person;
second, the absence of the mark of phenomena.
There are three aspects of the conceptualization of emptiness as non-apprehension.
There are likewise three aspects of wishlessness;
because these three aspects are empty, there are no three wishes.
Because they share the same lack of intrinsic nature, they are said to accord with emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
This applies equally to the other two; thus, one should understand that they correspond to one another.
This principle extends to all phenomena, which are entirely subsumed within the three types of emptiness.
The seven subsequent lines clarify that objects are empty within space.
The first four lines directly explain their emptiness by addressing the very substance of the objects themselves;
the following line establishes emptiness in relation to the sense faculties.
Next, there is one phrase that clarifies emptiness by referring to the substance of the objects (*viṣaya*);
the final phrase clarifies emptiness by referring to consciousness (*vijñāna*).
Regarding the first phrase, "the phenomena (*dharma*) are free from the beautiful and the ugly":
Yuan said: "This clarifies the absence of characteristics.
Within the boundaries of phenomena, dust may be beautiful or foul."
A good reputation is called "beautiful," while a bad reputation is called "ugly.
Because the true Dharma is free from these, it possesses neither beauty nor ugliness.
Zhuang said:
"Wholesome dharmas are good;
unwholesome ones are ugly."
The Dharma has neither good nor evil;
how could there be beauty or ugliness? Ruyi said:
True wisdom is beautiful;
ignorance is ugly. The true nature of phenomena is emptiness.
"What is beautiful? What is ugly?
The Dharma has neither increase nor decrease. Yuan said.
This clarifies the function of being free from defilements.
That which is favorable and beneficial is termed "increase" (*vṛddhi*); that which is contrary to one's feelings is called "decrease" (*hāni*).
The true Dharma is free from these [distinctions]; thus it is said to be without increase or decrease.
Zhiyi says: "If there were arising, there would be increase."
If there were cessation, there would be diminution;
since dharmas are without arising or cessation, they are free from increase and decrease.
Master Zhuang said:
The markless true Dharma exists whether there is a Buddha or no Buddha;
its nature is eternally abiding and possesses no dual characteristics.
Thus, the Tathāgata preaches the Dharma to universally deliver all sentient beings.
The dharma of cessation does not decrease,
nor does nirvana increase.
Dharmas are without arising or ceasing.
The fact that dharmas have no place of return clarifies that their essence is free from the six sense-objects.
Since the essence of the six sense-objects arises and ceases,
they are described as subject to birth and death.
That which belongs to persons is called "returning.
Since the true Dharma is detached from these, it is without arising or ceasing, and likewise has no place to which it returns.
It is further said:
Arising and ceasing follow from conditions and lack inherent nature;
though they arise, they do not arise,
and though they cease, they do not cease.
If dharmas were subject to arising, they would necessarily return to cessation;
because they are without arising, they do not return to cessation.
Dharmas transcend the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
In terms of correlating the objects with the six sense faculties to clarify the emptiness of those objects:
within the limits of phenomenal reality, the six sense-objects are the domains traversed by the six sense-faculties;
for the followers of the Two Vehicles, these are not yet termed "transcended."
In reality, there are no defilements.
Because the eyes and other faculties cannot reach it, it is called "transcendent.
As for the fact that phenomena have neither high nor low and are eternally abiding and immovable:
Returning to the substance of the sensory objects (*viṣaya*) to define their emptiness:
within the boundaries of phenomenal things, these objects possess degrees of superiority and inferiority;
those of the higher realms are superior and thus "high."
The dust of the lower realms is inferior and thus considered "low";
the three realms are all empty.
Since the true Dharma is free from these, there is neither high nor low.
Furthermore, one does not exalt oneself when among the noble,
nor do one debase oneself when among the ordinary;
for the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is equal in essence, being without high or low.
Birth and death are low;
nirvana is high. Within the dharma of emptiness, because there is no birth and death, there is no low.
Because there is no nirvana, there is no loftiness.
Because it is eternally abiding and immovable, it is explained as being without high or low.
Thus, the Dharma is detached from the practitioner of contemplation.
Distinguishing emptiness by way of consciousness:
within the limits of phenomena, atoms serve as the conditions for consciousness;
this does not depart from contemplative practice.
Within the true Dharma, there is no object-dust (rajas) to be perceived;
therefore, it is called "free from all modes of contemplative practice" (sarva-vipaśyanā-caryā-vivikta).
Question:
Since the true dharma is already free from contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*),
does non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) not take suchness (*tathatā*) as its object?
He replied:

"Detached from the practitioner of contemplation" means being detached from the mind of conceptual contemplation belonging to ordinary beings and the two vehicles, which takes the true as its object but fails to reach what is expressed by that term.
If one considers it in relation to true wisdom, even when taking [the true] as its object, it is not detached from practice.
It may be so. Although non-conceptual wisdom takes suchness as its object, it is nonetheless free from discursive observation. Why is this?
When wisdom realizes suchness, it does not grasp at the characteristics of suchness;
therefore, it is said to be "detached. Alternatively, this may be understood as follows:
Although wisdom takes suchness as its object,
it has no object to be apprehended;
it is likewise free from the activity of contemplation.
The above constitutes the Separate Teaching (*pratyekayāna*).
As for the phrase, "Such are the characteristics of phenomena;
how could they be described?", this is a reprimand from the standpoint of ultimate principle, restating the names and dharmas previously analyzed.
This is called the state where both name and form are utterly transcended and mental activity is likewise absent;
how could it possibly be proclaimed?
Thus far, the teaching has been presented by way of the essential nature of the Dharma being taught.
From here below is the second section, which teaches by means of the ritual for the speaker.
Within this, there are three parts.
First, the ritual for speaking.
Second, being free from faults and endowed with virtues;
third, exhortation.
Regarding the first, the ritual for the discourse, there are two parts.
First, the Dharma;
second, the analogy.
Within the Dharma, there is neither speaking nor showing.
Yuan said: "It clarifies that there is no person who speaks.
To take words and set them against the Dharma is what is called 'speaking'."
The proclamation of the Dharma is shown by means of names;
yet within the ultimate principle, these names do not exist and there is no verbal demonstration.
As for those who listen to the Dharma:
"Neither hearing nor attaining" clarifies that there is no person who hears.
To respond to speech with the ear is called "hearing";
to understand the Dharma through hearing is called "attaining."
In principle, there is no such thing as "attainment through non-hearing.
As the proverb says:
"One who expounds the Dharma clarifies that phenomena are not non-existent."
The absence of speech and the absence of demonstration manifest that phenomena are not existent;
because they are not existent, they are free from permanence; because they are not non-existent, they are free from annihilation.
That which is neither existent nor non-existent is the departure from the extremes of annihilation and permanence;
this is called the correct teaching.
Those who listen to the Dharma understand that phenomena are not non-existent.
Without hearing and without attaining, one manifests that phenomena are not existent;
being non-existent, one is free from permanence, and being non-nonexistent, one is free from annihilation.
To be free from both annihilation and permanence is called "right hearing."
Furthermore, it is said:
because that which is spoken transcends words, it is called "no speaking";
yet, one points out the Dharma to others by means of it.
The true nature of phenomena is emptiness;
it demonstrates that which cannot be demonstrated,
and is therefore called "non-demonstration."
Regarding "neither hearing nor attaining":
one constantly hears the True Dharma;
because the essence of the Dharma is empty, it is said that there is no hearing.
Based on hearing, one realizes;
one realizes the true Dharma.
The intrinsic nature of phenomena is emptiness.
Because one attains yet does not attain, it is called "non-attainment.
Cè (Cèlún) says:
"The dharma-body of the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa) is nameless; therefore, it cannot be spoken of."
Because it is signless, it cannot be demonstrated;
because it is ineffable, there is no hearing;
because it cannot be demonstrated, there is no attainment.
Furthermore, it is said:
Because the teaching of all phenomena is without substantial teaching, it is called "non-teaching.
Because the showing of phenomena to others is without substantial showing, it is called "non-showing."
Hearing the True Dharma with the ears is called "no hearing" because there is no real hearing;
realizing the mind and attaining the Dharma is called "no attainment" because there is no real attainment.
This is the relinquishing of pervasive conceptualization and emotional attachment.
Therefore, the Vimalakīrti Sūtra states:
"Indeed, those who preach the Dharma all engage in superimposition and denial;
likewise, those who listen to the Dharma also all engage in superimposition and denial."
Zhuang said:
"Among those who preach the Dharma, there are many who manifest the aspect of the mind;
among the disciples who listen to the Dharma, all possess the aspect of hearing and attaining it."
Now, as for those who preach the Dharma, there is no preaching and no demonstrating;
though they discourse all day long, they have never actually spoken,
and though they instruct and guide all day long, they have never shown anything to others.
It is not that one closes the mouth and neither speaks nor shows;
rather, those who listen to the Dharma neither hear nor attain it.
Though they listen to the Dharma all day long, they have never heard it.
Like the ocean swallowing rivers,
it has never failed to receive them;
it is not that one fails to hear because one plugs one's ears and refuses to listen.
It is not that there is no attainment at all that constitutes "non-attainment.
This is truly because the listener is ultimately pure. Thus, the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra* (or *Saṃghāṭa-sūtra*, here referred to as the *Siyi jing*) says:
If there is a bodhisattva among this assembly who thinks,
"Now this Dharma is being taught," you should know that such a person is not truly listening to the Dharma.
Why is this? Because one who does not listen to the Dharma is truly listening to the Dharma.
It is like a phantom person preaching the Dharma for a phantom person.
One should establish this intention:
when the teacher of the Dharma uses this analogy, it illustrates that, like an illusory person, there is no speaker;
and that teaching the Dharma to an illusory person illustrates that there is no listener.
It is not meant that because dharmas lack names and marks, there is no teaching.
For those who listen, the natures of person and self are empty;
who, then, would be the one to teach?
Those who hear it should maintain this perspective:
it is as if a phantom were preaching to a phantom.
Having explained this, the second section clarifies the excellence of his teaching of the Dharma.
Reversing the previous four faults to clarify the four virtues:
"One should understand the faculties" refers first to the virtue of the Dharma-preacher knowing the faculties [of others].
"Because he clearly understands the sharpness or dullness of the faculties of sentient beings.
"Skilled in knowledge and vision" refers to the second point:
clarifying the virtue of realizing the Dharma.
Because they have realized the profound Dharma, they are free from all obstructions.
Regarding the third point, the illumination of the virtue of great compassion:
it is because they skillfully expound the Mahāyāna for the sake of sentient beings.
The Dharma of the Mahāyāna uproots suffering at its very source;
this is why it gives rise to compassion.
To repay the Buddha’s kindness is as follows:

Having erroneously distinguished between the heterodox and the orthodox, one abandons poverty to beg from the wealthy;

Third, from "Having spoken this Dharma... onwards, it clarifies the benefit of the instruction and reprimand.
Regarding the reason why Vimalakīrti took the bowl and filled it with food while reproaching [Śāriputra]:
Why did the Pure Name (Vimalakīrti) take the bowl and fill it with food yet not give it to him?
Briefly, there are three reasons.
First, take the bowl as the means to end the dispute;
if you do not take the bowl,
he will abandon the discussion out of fear of being subjected to further challenges and intimidation.
Second, fearing that giving less than full measure would incur the fault of stinginess,

Third, by relying on alms for sustenance, he established the basis for initiating discourse.
Therefore, he first took his bowl and filled it with rice.
Now, Subhūti, the following section clearly explains the formal instruction and reprimand;

second, not abandoning lustful conduct is inequality regarding bondage and liberation;

The four types of entry into false views fall short of equality regarding all phenomena.
By reversing these four faults, the teaching establishes the four virtues.
This constitutes a general reprimand intended to turn back and rebuke Subhūti.
If you have truly attained the samādhi of emptiness and non-contention,

Do not give rise to discrimination.

turning your back on those heterodox teachers to take refuge in the Buddha’s True Dharma is precisely what constitutes a contradiction.

If one wishes to accord with that Great Emptiness, the Samādhi of Equality and Non-contention, [one must proceed as follows].
One must not perceive the beauty or ugliness of food;

If one can act in this manner, then one may take the food.
Regarding the first section on the inequality of food, there are three distinct points:

Second, by means of the food of dharma and inference;
