Subhūti alone is equal regarding food and all other dharmas.
This is the first phrase:
"You now abandon poverty for wealth;
you perceive the good and evil of food."
One immediately knows that there is inequality regarding food;
yet all phenomena share the same characteristic, taking the nature of reality (dharmatā) as their true essence.
One thus knows that you are unequal regarding the Dharma.
Furthermore, by applying this method to the category of food,
observing that the substance of food is empty is called "equality of food.
By analogy with this, one applies it to other categories, which is called "equality of phenomena" (*dharma-samatā*).
Regarding "all phenomena are equal":
the second line uses the category of phenomena as the object of contemplation;
observing that the nature of phenomena is empty and devoid of defilement or purity is called "phenomena are equal."
Food of this kind is called "food" and is likewise equal [to other food].
Thus, when begging for alms, one may take such food;
this third phrase concludes the permission to accept food.
Since all phenomena share the same characteristic, they may be understood by analogy with one; if one is equanimous toward both dharmas and food,
then begging for alms through this practice constitutes a field of merit,
and it is thus permissible to accept food.
"Regarding 'one may take food, etc.':
this refers to taking the exquisite food of the wealthy and so forth, as well as the filthy meals of the poor.
If one can [remain equanimous] toward such coarse or exquisite food,"
One is thus able to be equanimous toward all phenomena;
if one realizes that the myriad dharmas are all equal,
one is then able to be equanimous toward food as well.
One who attains such a mind is a true field of merit;
only then may one accept food.
One does not sever lust, anger, and ignorance, yet does not dwell together with them.
Second, there are ten points concerning how Subhūti’s critique of bondage and liberation as being unequal is incorrect:
"If you have attained the wisdom of the equality of emptiness..."
For what reason? Because one has severed the three poisons and abandoned the view of a self-identity;
because delusion, craving, views, and evil karma have been extinguished; because the bonds of existence have been released;
and because, having seen the Four Noble Truths, one clings to the attainment of the fruit.
To distance oneself from ordinary beings while grasping at the state of a sage and becoming attached to all phenomena—
these are the ten matters by which it is known that you do not understand the equality of all phenomena.
Among these ten, the first nine are specific and the last one is general.
Within the first nine, the initial seven are formulated by way of their practice.
The latter two are explained in terms of the person to whom they refer.
Within the former [five], the first five constitute the virtue of abandonment (*prahāṇa-guṇa*),
while the latter two constitute the virtue of wisdom (*jñāna-guṇa*).
This is also acceptable.
The first five abandon defilement;
the latter two cultivate purity.
Among the first five, the first three involve the abandonment of afflictions (*kleśa*),
the next one involves the abandonment of karma,
and the last one involves the abandonment of suffering (*duḥkha*).
Among the afflictions, the first two are delusions of view (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*),
and the last one is the delusion of cultivation (*bhāvanā-kleśa*). Within the delusions of view, the former is dull and the latter is sharp.
"Neither severing lust, anger, and ignorance, nor being accompanied by them" means that although the Buddha is free from the three poisons,
he constantly manifests in accordance with the needs of those he transforms; therefore,
it is said that he does not sever them.

"Nor does one associate with them" means that because one realizes the truth and looks back to see that what has come from the beginning was never existent, there is nothing with which one can associate.
It is not that one sees dharmas as existing and then abandons them, failing to associate with them.
Because they do not coexist, they are not the same as ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*);
because they are not abandoned, they are not the same as those of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*).
Other distinct categories are likewise [to be understood].
If explained according to the three natures (*trisvabhāva*),
the afflictions of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita*) are by nature originally empty; thus,
there are no delusions to be severed.
Therefore it is said that they are not severed.
Since there is nothing to be severed,
with whom could they coexist?
Second, when the afflictions of the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) are severed, it is not severed;
this is called "non-severance.
Because it is severed while being non-severed, it is said that they do not coexist.
The three perfections are the true nature, inherently pure and free from any delusion that could be severed;
therefore, it is said that "nothing is severed.
Since there is no delusion apart from the truth, with what could it coexist?
Therefore, it is said that they do not coexist.

If we consider the Bodhisattvas, from the first stage (*bhūmi*) upward, they manifest the discrimination of the three poisons in order to transform sentient beings; thus, it is said that they are not severed.
According to the principle, there is in fact nothing that can be called "not simultaneous.
Regarding the phrase "without destroying the body while conforming to a single mark," Yuan says:

Manifesting the view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) to teach and transform sentient beings without abandoning it is called the "indestructible body" (*akṣaya-kāya*), which accords with the single mark (*ekalakṣaṇa*).
In principle, this is the single mark; its practice and realization are called "following" (*anugata*).
The body is fundamentally empty by its very nature; this is precisely the single mark (ekalakṣaṇa).
Why, then, must one destroy the view of the body to conform to that single mark?
As the proverb says:
Suchness is equanimous and is termed the "one mark.
The aggregates and the body are empty; there is no dharma that can be destroyed.
This indestructibility is precisely Suchness, and is therefore called the "one mark."
"Why is it necessary to destroy the five aggregates (pañca-skandha) in order to follow a single characteristic?
This interpretation is incorrect;
the body itself is the view of a self (satkāya-dṛṣṭi), not the five aggregates."
It is further said:
"The śrāvaka attains the signless by extinguishing the body;
the Mahāsattva knows that the nature of the body is empty and thus perceives it as the single mark."
Why must one destroy the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) before conforming to a single characteristic?
Therefore, Vimalakīrti said:
"Without destroying the view of a self-identity, one conforms to a single characteristic."
Regarding the statement, "Without extinguishing delusion and craving, one gives rise to clarity and liberation," Yuan says:
"The 'afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation' refers to the latent tendencies of ignorance (*avidyā-anuśaya*)."
The failure to comprehend what has arisen is called delusion (*moha*).
Attachment to desire, attachment to form, and attachment to existence—abiding in these stages—is called craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
Because it continues to manifest in accordance with its transformations, it is said to be "unextinguished."
Regarding "arising of clarity and liberation":
clarity refers to the clarity of wisdom;
liberation refers to the liberation of the mind.
Because the ignorance of ordinary beings is thick, it can obstruct wisdom.
In the case of the two vehicles, ignorance is partially removed;
when ignorance is severed, wisdom becomes luminous, craving is extinguished, and the mind is liberated.
The Bodhisattva is not like this;
they realize that ignorance and craving have been non-existent from the beginning,
which is itself clarity and liberation.
Zhaò said: "The śrāvakas have ignorance that obstructs wisdom;
only by extinguishing ignorance does wisdom become clear."
The mind is bound by craving;
only by removing craving is one liberated.
The Great Being realizes that the nature of delusion and craving is empty.
This is precisely what clarifies liberation.
Who binds the mind that one must then extinguish?
Or perhaps it may be so.
Delusion and craving are themselves innate confusion;
their distinct activities arise with superficial and proximate characteristics.
That which the Tathāgata manifests as activity is called "non-extinction."
The arising of unobstructed wisdom is called "clarity" (*vidyā*).
Regarding those who attain liberation by being freed from the characteristics of the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya*),
this is next explained in terms of karma.
Killing one's father, harming one's mother, killing an Arhat, causing a schism in the Saṃgha, and shedding the blood of a Buddha—
these are the five ānantarya offenses.
Because these acts involve ingratitude and rebellion against the field of merit, they are designated as "ānantarya" (immediate).
Killing one's father and mother is a transgression because it involves betraying their kindness;
the latter three are transgressions because they involve betraying the field of merit.
These are termed the five characteristics of the heinous crimes (ānantarya) according to how they manifest through transformation.
Those who attain liberation are said to have achieved "liberation" because they have forever severed the fetters of karma.
Furthermore, it is said that followers of the Hīnayāna regard evil karma as an obstacle.
One must sever [these bonds] to attain liberation.
A practitioner of the Mahāyāna knows that karma arises from conditions,
and that the nature of conditions is itself empty.
How can karma exist?
Because emptiness does not act as an obstruction, it is called liberation;
this refers to liberation through the emptiness of unwholesome karma.
Furthermore, regarding the clear elucidation of the five heinous crimes:
one kills the father of ignorance and severs the mother of craving.
The Buddha who ceases and eliminates the deluded consciousness that perceives objects;
the Arhat who slays the fetters and afflictions;
the Saṃgha that destroys the accumulation of the aggregates.
To be able to commit these five heinous crimes is itself true liberation.
Regarding the statement "neither bound nor liberated," this refers to the retribution of suffering.
Yuǎn says: The Tathāgata is called "unbound" because he is not entangled by the retributive suffering of birth and death;
he is called "unreleased" because he manifests his conduct in accordance with transformative teachings.
Furthermore, Manzhiu said:
"For those of the Two Vehicles, karmic obstructions constitute their bondage;
by removing them, they attain liberation."
The Bodhisattva knows that the nature of phenomena is empty and fundamentally unbound;
since there is no binding, [there is no liberation].
He then provided an explanation:
"The Bodhisattva who attains sudden enlightenment, prior to the seventh stage, has not yet abandoned the分段 (fen-duan) [body] and is thus termed 'not yet liberated' (bù jiě).
Having realized that the nature of dharmas is empty, he is termed 'unbound' (bù fù)."
Therefore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"It is not that Bodhisattvas do not possess suffering;
rather, understanding that suffering is without suffering is called the Noble Truth of Suffering."
Furthermore, the subsequent scripture states:
"If there were originally no bondage,
who would seek liberation?"
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"Because it is empty, because it is detached, because it is quiescent, and because it is unarisen, there is neither bondage nor liberation. Alternatively, it may be interpreted thus.
Because a Bodhisattva of gradual enlightenment manifests in the segmented existence (*paricchinna-bhava*) to transform sentient beings, they are called "not yet liberated.
Having already abandoned the segmented existence, they are called "unbound. Alternatively, it may be understood thus: [text fragment].
Not having abandoned the transformation-death (pariṇāmi-cyuti) is called "not liberated.
Understanding that the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is empty is called "unbound.
Thus far, we have explained the virtue of abandonment (prahāṇa-guṇa) in terms of defilement and criticized [the opponent] for their inequality.
The following two lines clarify their wisdom and virtue through purity and reproach them for their inequality.
The first line refers to the cause;
the second refers to the fruit.
"Neither seeing the truths nor not seeing the truths" refers to the cause.
When the Tathāgata manifests the arising of views and doubts while not contemplating the principle of the truths, this is called "not seeing";
yet because he internally realizes and understands them in reality, it is called "not not seeing."
This is the general designation for the mode of activity on the stages (*bhūmi*), which does not involve the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana*).
If one considers the bodhisattvas who attain awakening gradually,
from the first stage up to the tenth stage, they manifest the arising of views and doubts in order to transform sentient beings.
Therefore, it is called "not seeing the truths.
However, because one internally realizes them in reality, it is not the case that they are not seen; this may be understood in such a way.
For Bodhisattvas on the seven stages and below, the fact that they retain latent afflictions (*anuśaya*) and do not contemplate the principles of the truths is called "not seeing.
However, because they internally and actually realize [the truth], it is not called "not seeing."
If one considers the realization of the true essence through wisdom:
because wisdom is free from the discrimination of subject and object, it is called "not seeing";
yet because it clearly illuminates the two kinds of emptiness, it is not "not seeing."
Alternatively, it may be so:
correct wisdom arises from conditions;
because conditions lack intrinsic nature, there is nothing seen to be seen.
It is called "not seeing.
To have no seeing as one's seeing is what is meant by "not not seeing.
If subsequent knowledge (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) is free from attachment and conceptual discrimination, it is called "not seeing."
To discern and illuminate the Four Noble Truths is not called "not seeing.
Zhuangzi said:
"The followers of the Two Vehicles see the Truths, while ordinary beings do not."
The Bodhisattva knows that the nature of the Four Noble Truths is empty and enters the principle of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
Therefore, he is free from both views and non-views.
Sengzhao says:
It is not like seeing with a mind,
nor is it like not seeing without a mind;
it is not the attainment of a fruit.
This is explained in terms of the fruit. Yuan says:
"These words are too brief; following the previous pattern, one should have said..."
It is not that one attains the fruit, nor is it that one does not attain the fruit;
this is merely citing one side of the matter.
Bodhi and Nirvana are termed "fruits. However,
because the Buddha realized Bodhi yet continued to perform the deeds of a cause—
never abandoning any of the practices of a bodhisattva— it is said that he did not "attain" the fruit.
Because one has actually realized bodhi, it is not the case that it is not attained;
this is not discussed in detail here.
As the proverb says:
Because the Dharma is free from subject and object, it is said that "no fruit is attained.
This does not mean that no fruit is attained; rather, it is because the person and the Dharma are not identical. Pūrṇa said:
Ordinary beings do not attain the fruit;
śrāvakas attain the fruit.
Bodhisattvas skillfully penetrate that the essence of the fruit is itself empty, having never existed from the outset.
Why say it cannot be attained?
It is not that it is unattainable; rather, it may be so.
Bodhisattvas from the first bhūmi upward realize non-abiding nirvāṇa, which is called "attaining the fruit.
This realized wisdom arises from conditions;
yet the nature of those conditions is itself empty.
One realizes that there is nothing to be realized;
therefore, it is said that no fruit is attained. Alternatively, it may be understood thus.
When [the fruit] is attained, one is free from attachment and does not give rise to discrimination; thus it is said "not attaining the fruit.
This does not mean that it is not attained at all.
The commentaries of the ancients all state that the translators of the sutras omitted the latter part of the sentence.
In truth, there ought to be two phrases;
however, the examination of the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa* reveals that there is only the phrase "not attaining the fruit.
Even if this was an omission, it occurred at the time of the compilation [of the canon].
Alternatively,
it may be that the latter phrase does not exist in the Sanskrit original.
"Not an ordinary person, yet separated from the dharmas of an ordinary person."
The final two phrases are addressed to people for the purpose of reproof:
because he possesses the inner preparation of sagely virtue, he is not an ordinary person;
yet because he manifests in all affairs to transform sentient beings, he is not apart from being an ordinary person.
Furthermore, it is said:
"A Bodhisattva who has attained sudden enlightenment, from the first stage up to the seventh stage, has already acquired the nature of a sage and is thus no longer an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).
By the power of intentional effort (*saṃcetanīya-vaśa*), they arouse afflictions (*kleśa*) to assist their compassionate vows (*karuṇā-praṇidhāna*) and thereby undergo rebirth."
It is not that they are separated from ordinary dharmas.
If one remains with the seeds of greed and so forth upon reaching the eighth stage and above,
it is not that they are separated from the dharmas of ordinary beings.

If one considers the Bodhisattvas of gradual enlightenment who, from the first stage (*bhūmi*) upward, have already realized the nature of the noble ones (*ārya-gotra*), they are no longer called ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
Nevertheless, because they manifest afflictions (*kleśa*) in order to transform sentient beings, they are not separated from the dharmas of ordinary beings.
Regarding "neither a sage nor not a sage":
the Tathāgata manifests as an ordinary person to transform sentient beings, and is thus called "not a sage.
This is spoken according to worldly convention.
It is not that they are not sages.
Furthermore, while the śrāvakas have not yet been able to eliminate their mental attachments and grasp at the characteristics of a sage,
the practitioners of the Mahāyāna realize that the nature of a sage is empty.
How is it that one takes up the marks of the noble and does not take up the marks of the non-noble?
The preceding section concludes the individual inquiries.
Although one accomplishes all dharmas, it is only by being detached from the marks of all dharmas that one may partake of the food.
This single phrase serves as a general conclusion and exhortation;
it clarifies that because all phenomena perish at the very moment they are formed, they are termed "detached.
If one is as described above—attaining only gain and never loss—then one may accept food.
"If Subhūti does not see the Buddha" marks the third section, which rebukes Subhūti for inequality regarding the Teacher and the Dharma;
it is also said to concern the inequality between the heterodox and the orthodox.
This passage contains four parts.
First, a general inquiry;
second, the differing views arising from the six teachers;
third, a further inquiry and reprimand.
The four points regarding the permission to accept food are as follows:
the initial statement, "I have neither seen the Buddha nor heard the Dharma," serves as a general inquiry that turns back to reprimand Śāriputra.
If you have truly attained the samādhi of emptiness,
why did you not previously see the Buddha or hear the Dharma like the six heretical teachers?
Why is it that you have now abandoned those heretical views to see the Buddha as your teacher and listen to the Buddha’s true Dharma?
In this case, acceptance and rejection have not yet been extinguished;
how, then, can it be called the samādhi of emptiness?
Master Zhuang said:

Those of the two vehicles claim that abandoning the state of an ordinary person and attaining the state of a sage must depend upon seeing the Buddha and hearing the Dharma; this [passage] refutes such a view.
Subhūti himself claimed to have seen the Buddha and heard the Dharma, yet here he says that he neither saw nor heard.
These words appear to contradict their underlying principle of the true nature of reality (*dharmatā*).
If there were a Buddha to be seen, that would constitute "seeing," and thus one would not be seeing the Buddha.
If there were a Dharma to be heard, that would constitute "hearing," and thus it would not be hearing the Dharma.

Now, it is clarified that the non-existence of a Buddha who can be seen is precisely what is called "seeing the Buddha," and the non-existence of a Dharma that can be heard is what is called "hearing the Dharma.
This is intended to refute the [notions of] existence held by the followers of the Two Vehicles.
Therefore, it is said that [the Buddha] does not exist.
Once one knows that the Buddha is not existent,
one then realizes that the Buddha is not non-existent.
When these five phrases are free from all attachment, this is the beginning of the Dharmakāya; awakening to it in this manner is called "seeing the Buddha.
Thus, the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* says:
Those whose false views are deep-seated claim that there is no Tathāgata;
yet even to differentiate the Tathāgata’s mark of quiescence as existing is incorrect.
Within the initial section on the lower categories, the six heterodox teachers are first introduced to show how their arising of views differs from what precedes.
Pūraṇa is his name; Kāśyapa is his clan.
This person has given rise to the view of annihilationism.
He asserts that all phenomena are empty and devoid of the way of ruler and minister, father and son, loyalty and filial piety.
"Makkhali" is his name; "Gosāla" is the name of his mother.
This person gives rise to the view of eternalism,
asserting that all suffering and pleasure do not arise from karma but exist inherently by their own nature.
"Saṃjaya" is his name.
The name of Pūraṇa Kāśyapa’s mother;
this person gives rise to the view of spontaneity,
maintaining that the Path need not be cultivated.
When the suffering of eighty thousand kalpas is exhausted, one is spontaneously liberated;
it is like a ball of thread unwinding on a high mountain— it stops of its own accord when the thread is finished,
yet this is not the cause of liberation.
To call this a cause is to regard what is not a cause as a cause; this is the view of clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).
To deny the Path and claim that the Path need not be cultivated is wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).
"Ājīva" is his name.
"Kāśyapa" is a term for coarse, worn-out clothing;
he was an ascetic non-Buddhist.
Tearing out one's own hair and scorching the body with five fires to attain liberation—
this is also the clinging to precepts (śīlavrataparāmarśa), which regards what is not the Path as the Path. Kālāma is his name.
Kātyāyana is his clan name.
This person gives rise to extreme views,
clinging to the notion that all phenomena both exist and do not exist.
This is not the same as the Buddha-dharma.
Because of causes and conditions it exists; because of its lack of intrinsic nature it does not exist.
This is right view, not an extreme view.
To grasp at existence as being an existence with a fixed nature is the view of eternalism;
to speak of non-existence as being a non-existence with a fixed nature is the view of nihilism.
The segments constantly deviate from the center;
their combination constitutes the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*). This is the term *nirgrantha*.
This person, known by the name Puttamāṇava,
asserts that all fruits of suffering and happiness arise solely from past karma and do not depend on present conditions; thus,
when the karma of previous lives is exhausted, suffering is likewise exhausted.
Even if they were to manifest the path of cultivation, it could not sever [the afflictions].
This person believes that past karma serves as the cause;
they do not falsely deny the existence of present conditions.
This constitutes a partial wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).
To deny that the Path can bring an end to suffering by claiming it cannot do so,
or to regard what is not the Path as the Path, is likewise wrong view.
These six teachers are fully described in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
"Three are your teachers" and so forth refers to the subsequent re-examination that overturns heterodoxy to enter into the correct path.
Subhūti understands emptiness and equality, wherein there is neither heterodoxy nor correctness.
Since these two characteristics are absent,
one is identical to the non-Buddhists;
one neither sees the Buddha nor hears the Dharma.
This means that one receives the Way from a teacher of false views;
because of him, one leaves the household life in error.
Since that teacher has fallen into the three evil realms, [the disciple likewise follows].
One cannot help but follow where one falls;
only if one can act in this way will one be able to perceive with impartiality.
You have now turned away from the six teachers and abandoned their false teachings.
I know that you have not yet abandoned conceptual discrimination and have not attained equanimity;
how, then, can you be said to understand emptiness?
If you can neither turn away from nor abandon the equanimity of all phenomena, [only then do you understand emptiness].
This is precisely the liberation from emptiness.
Only then may one partake of food; the four fetters permit the taking of food.
When one's conduct accords with equality, this is itself the field of merit.
Only then may one partake of the food.

This concludes the fourth section, "Entering Various False Views and Not Reaching the Other Shore," which rebukes Subhūti for his inequality regarding all dharmas and establishes the perfection of virtue through interrogation.
The text contains eleven phrases,
which are divided into three sections in meaning.
The first section consists of one phrase, clarifying that [the view] is identical to that of the non-Buddhists (tīrthika).
Next, there are five phrases that clarify how [you] are the same as ordinary worldlings. Following that, there are five phrases that clarify how [you] are the same as the various Māras.

As for the general intent of this censure: how could you possibly attain the correct path? You have encountered the eight difficulties (*aṣṭāv akṣaṇāḥ*), seen defilement and purity, and failed to realize their equality; you have grasped at fields with partiality, perceived transgressions and blessings, and emerged from the realm of Māra only to become distinct from the Māras themselves. You feel compassion for sentient beings while being attached to the Three Jewels, and so on, up to the eleventh point: you claim to have realized nirvāṇa through direct vision, yet now you cannot enter the state of non-attainment; you dwell amidst the eight difficulties, are equal to afflictions, and remain in a state of contention, failing even to grasp cessation. For these reasons, it is known that you have not yet attained the samādhi of emptiness and non-contention (*araṇā*); because you do not yet know this, I have instead instructed and censured you.
Regarding those who have first entered various false views and have not reached the other shore:
the first section clarifies their commonality with non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*),
thereby refuting Subhūti’s grasping at the characteristics of the false and the correct.
The "other shore" is nirvana.
In the Hīnayāna, false views are regarded as the "this shore" and [the absence of] false views as the "right other shore.
Therefore, one abandons these false views and returns to the other shore.
The practitioner of the Mahāyāna knows that the nature of false views is empty.
How can there be emergence from them? How can there be nirvāṇa and cessation?
How can one arrive [at it]?
The nature of false views and the other shore are not different.
Why then abandon the false and rejoice in the other shore?
Therefore, one enters into false views without reaching the other shore.
It further states:
"In order to transform sentient beings, he enters into various false views, does not abide in nirvana, and does not reach the other shore.
From here below is the second section, clarifying the text on being the same as ordinary beings, which contains five parts.
First, it destroys the attainment of the eight difficult conditions;
second, it destroys the grasping at the marks of defilement and purity;
third, it destroys the unevenness of the concentrated mind.
Fourth, the characteristic of destroying the field of merit;
fifth, the characteristic of destroying the grasping of sin and merit.
To dwell in the eight difficulties and not obtain freedom from difficulty.
First, one breaks down the characteristics of the eight difficulties.
Now, one who perceives difficulty as difficult will necessarily abandon difficulty and seek the absence of difficulty.
If one can, however, not regard difficulty as difficulty, [then there is no abandonment].
One is able to abide in what is difficult,
yet because one does not regard it as difficult, one does not fail to attain the state of being free from difficulty;
for the nature of difficulty is itself empty.
How can one abandon [the eight difficulties] so as to attain freedom from them?
Furthermore, it is said:
"In order to transform those dwelling within the eight difficulties, [one remains there]."
"Not clinging to bodhi and not dwelling in the absence of difficulty" means being identical with afflictions while remaining detached from pure dharmas;
this second point refutes the grasping at the marks of defilement and purity.
In order to transform sentient beings, he manifests as being identical to their afflictions;
thus, he does not cling to nirvana and remains detached from the dharmas of purity.
Or it is said:
The followers of the two vehicles eliminate defilement to attain purity;
yet that very purity becomes defiled once again.
The Bodhisattva, however, realizes that defilement is not truly defilement.
That which is defiled is eternally pure;
therefore, it is identical to afflictions in its departure from purity.
Thus, the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-samādhi-sūtra* (Siyi jing) says:
Sometimes defiled phenomena are described as pure, and pure phenomena are described as defiled.
How is it that pure phenomena are described as defiled?
Because of attachment to pure phenomena.
How is it that defiled phenomena are said to be pure?
Because one does not perceive defiled phenomena.
Furthermore, the subsequent sutra states:
When one perceives the true nature of defilement, there is no characteristic of purity.
As for your claim that "if you attain the Samādhi of Non-contention,
sentient beings will also attain it," this third point refutes the inequality of the concentrated mind.
There are two kinds of non-contention (*araṇā*): first, non-contention in action, which,
by the power of samādhi, protects sentient beings so that they do not give rise to contention.
Sujīva said: "If anyone objects to my sitting, I shall stand;
if anyone objects to my being here, I shall depart."
Ultimately, there is no arising of contention.
Second, there is no contention in principle:
the true suchness and the dharma-nature are without opposition or contention.
It is by realizing the principle that one attains non-contention regarding phenomena.
Subhūti, you are equal to the principle of the emptiness of all sentient beings.
"Why is it that only Śubhavyūha alone attains the state of being 'without strife' (araṇā) while sentient beings do not?
This clarifies that the nature [of all beings] is fundamentally equal;
therefore, it is said that "sentient beings also attain it."
Regarding the statement, "One who gives to you is not called a field of merit," this is the fourth refutation of grasping at the marks of merit.
The intention of Subhūti is as follows:
I receive their offerings and cause them to attain great merit; therefore, I am called "merit.
Ordinary beings, upon receiving offerings, cannot cause those donors to obtain great merit, for they are not fields of merit.
You and ordinary beings are equal and identical in emptiness.
"How is it that ordinary persons are not fields of merit? Are you a field of merit?
Furthermore, when one contemplates that self and other are no different, who is the one possessing merit and who is the field?
Therefore it is said: "One who bestows [offerings] upon you is not called a field of merit. Yuan says:
"Lacking the virtue to benefit others, such a person is a worldly sinner; those who provide for them receive no merit."
Making offerings to you would be like that;
it does not produce merit,
and thus you are called one who is not a field of merit.
A proverb says:
"To practice giving based on appearances is not called making offerings to a field of merit with equanimity."
"Offerings made to you who have fallen into the three evil realms.
Fifth, [this concerns] the refutation of the marks of sin and merit. Man states:
Regarding the harm caused by the five heinous crimes and the benefit derived from making offerings, Śubhavyūha thought:
"Those who make offerings to me shall be reborn in the heavens."
Now, I shall respond with a rebuke:
Since their nature is empty and equal, where good and evil are non-dual,
how can it be that by practicing virtue one alone attains birth in heaven, while by committing sins one enters the evil realms?
If one were to fall into [hell] for committing the five heinous crimes,
then making offerings should likewise cause one to fall; yet since making offerings does not cause one to fall, [the former must be false].
Even those who have committed the five heinous crimes do not fall [into hell].
This may be called the simultaneous disappearance of both good and evil, wherein nature is empty and all things are equal.
Therefore, the sutra below says:
If one realizes the nature of sin, it is no different from merit.
As the proverb says:
"Though one may gain a small amount of merit through making offerings while grasping at signs, one will ultimately fall into the evil realms."
From here below, the third section clarifies the passage on being identical with the multitudes of Māras, which consists of five sentences:
first, destroying [the notion of] exiting the realm of Māra;
second, destroying [the notion of] being distinct from Māra.
Third, destroying compassion for sentient beings;
fourth, destroying attachment to the Triple Gem;
fifth, destroying the attainment of nirvāṇa.
Regarding the statement that "in the past he acted as a companion to Māra," Subhūti’s intention was that [the Buddha] first broke out from the realm of Māra.
I am a sage who has emerged from the realm of Māra;
now you have caused me to return to the same demonic activities as the various Māras, that is, the various Māra kings.
Māra is exclusively intent on causing disorder.
Because his actions are identical to those of Māra, they are called "shared.
It is like when people of the world create things with one hand; it is similar to saying that it is the work of a single hand.
That Māra can cause disturbance;
this is called "weariness.
To associate with him is to become his companion.
They are called companions in toil.
Since the nature of Māra is itself empty,
why must one abandon him and not dwell with him?
Having attained right view,
you are no different from the associates of Māra’s toil.
You are no different from the various Māras and the afflictions of worldly dust.
Second, [the opponent] argues that [the Māra-protectors] must differ from Māra;
yet, since they have become his companions,
how could they possibly be different?
You and the various māras are equal in the single emptiness, without two distinct characteristics;
how could you not be equal? Toward all sentient beings who harbor resentment toward you, [you should likewise maintain equanimity].
Third, it destroys compassion for sentient beings;
Māra can harm one's life of wisdom,
which is the most grievous of all enmities.
To give rise to that mind of loving-kindness is the meaning of "friend.
Sentient beings are empty of intrinsic nature.
"Enemies and kin are equal.
Since you are already able to arouse loving-kindness toward those who are equal,
why not do so for your enemies as well?"
Furthermore, those of the Hīnayāna speak only of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) to teach and transform sentient beings;
they thereby undermine the Mahāyāna for others.
To bestow the name of "Dharma-body" upon that which is merely a designation is called an enemy.
To slander the Buddha, destroy the Dharma, and not enter the assembly constitutes the fourth [transgression]:
the destruction of attachment to the Triple Gem.
"Subhūti, if you merely recite the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha and take pleasure in being counted among the multitude,
this is to grasp at the marks of the Triple Gem.
Since you are able to recite and praise them within that equality,"
Why would one slander?
Since one cannot slander,
how could one offer praise?
Thus, the *Acaranga Sūtra* states:
"Upon hearing the sound of praise for the Buddha, one immediately feels joy;
upon hearing the sound of disparagement of the Buddha, one immediately feels resentment."
One should know that such a person does not study the Buddha-dharma.
As a sutra says:
"The sounds of non-Buddhists are equal to the sounds of the Buddha."
It is further said:
"The Buddha’s teachings and false teachings are both without discrimination.
It is also said:

Those who slander the Buddha and destroy the Dharma do so because, despite their virtuous auspiciousness, they fail to realize that the Three Jewels are like space; by grasping at signs to offer praise, they deviate from the true essence.
Such people are precisely those who slander the Buddha, destroy the Dharma, and do not enter the ranks of the Sangha.
Therefore, the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra says:
"If one sees me by means of form, or seeks me by means of sound,
such a person walks upon a deviant path."
"Being unable to see the Tathāgata and ultimately failing to attain extinction" refers to the fifth [point]:
the refutation of the characteristics of realizing nirvāṇa.
The nature of sentient beings is empty and there is no one to be liberated;
yet now they attain nirvāṇa.
This is merely because those who possess signs cannot attain nirvāṇa.
Therefore, the *Buddhapiṭaka Sūtra* states:
"If a person perceives a fixed characteristic in nirvāṇa,
you should know that such a person is called a follower of external paths with evil and false views."
Furthermore, the subsequent scripture states:
"All sentient beings are themselves the mark of nirvana;
they do not undergo further extinction."
It is simply because the emptiness of the nature of sentient beings is itself nirvana.
How could one use nirvana to further realize nirvana?
It is also said:
Because Śubhūti’s mind is narrow and inferior, he cannot realize great parinirvāṇa;
therefore, he does not attain extinction.
Furthermore, it says:
Subhūti thought to himself,
"I am a noble one who has realized nirvāṇa," and so he now rebukes him.

In the emptiness of equality, one is free from both attainment and non-attainment; if you were to attain it, you would likewise not attain it. Since there is neither non-attainment nor attainment, only then may you take the food—this is the exhortation to resolve.
If you can now transcend the former notions of gain and loss and allow that which is destroyed to be empty and pervasive,
you are then a field of merit;
only then may you take this food.
Now, as for abandoning evil and following good, this is the common sentiment of humanity;
yet it does not penetrate the mind and remains unrelieved of its burdens.
Therefore, those who contemplate with equanimity regard the preservation of good as a source of affliction, and thus abandon good to seek the ultimate source;
they regard the rejection of evil as a burden, and thus encounter evil to return to the fundamental.
Thus, evil possesses the merit of non-entanglement,
while good possesses the achievement of non-defilement. Therefore,
we know that merely being "good" is not yet the attainment [of the ultimate].
"To share in evil is not yet a failure.
Does the meaning of the term "pure speech" (vimala-vāda) appear to be like this?
At that time, O World-Honored One, hearing this I was bewildered and did not know how to respond; I then set down my bowl and wished to leave his house.
The second part expresses one’s own humility and submission to demonstrate that the opponent is difficult to overcome.
This section contains two parts:
first, the obstruction of one’s own [pride].
Second, Vimalakīrti says: "Below, Viṣṇu (Net Name) employs the analogy to re-instruct through principle.
Within the former [section], 'bewildered' means that the internal mind is not clear."
Regarding the statement, "I do not know what these words mean, nor do I know how to answer them":
when one's speech returns to the scriptures and one's principles accord with the meaning,
because one has returned to the scriptures, one naturally asserts, "I do not know what these words mean."
Because it accords with the truth, I do not know how to answer;
what is below is excessive,
while what is above is insufficient.
Advancing or retreating, he lost his footing;
reflecting on how to respond, he found no way.

"Setting aside" means to relinquish.
In the second section, the teaching of Vimalakīrti consists of three parts: first the principle (*dharma*), then the analogy, and finally the application.
Regarding the principle, "take the bowl and do not fear" means:
Because Subhūti, due to being rebuked, felt such shame that he had no reply and discarded his bowl— thereby committing the fault of failing to speak—
Subhūti is now guided so that he may speak immediately and realize the intended meaning.
Therefore it is said: "Take the bowl without fear.
In the parable, when the Tathāgata’s created person (nirmāṇa-puruṣa) was thus questioned about the matter, would he have had any fear?
Although the created person heard these words, he was without mind.
Regarding the essence [of this], one wishes for Śubhūti to realize that he himself is like a magical transformation;
how could there be any fear?
Within the combined metaphors, there are two parts.
First the summary and then the explanation:
all phenomena are like illusions and transformations;
since there is nothing to fear, [one is fearless].
You, too, are like an illusion;
what cause for fear could there be? Why is this so?
The detailed explanation below consists of five statements.
The first statement— that all verbal expressions do not depart from these characteristics—
clarifies that one's own difficult words share the same nature as illusions and transformations.
Second, the wise person knows that transformations are unreal and therefore has nothing to fear.
Third, the section beginning with "For what reason" explains the underlying cause for neither being attached nor fearing:
because the substance of words is empty, it is said to be "naturally detached."
The convergence of the four assemblies is itself true liberation.
Now, names arise from insufficiency;
where there is sufficiency, there are no names.
Therefore, the absence of words is itself true liberation.
One should infer that all phenomena of the five categories possess the characteristic of liberation.
Furthermore, by understanding that both the internal and external are empty, one becomes free from all delusions.
Now, names arise from dharmas,
and dharmas arise from names; since names are already liberated, [dharmas are likewise liberated].
All dharmas are naturally liberated.
The benefit of this teaching is thus evident.
Therefore, I am unable to sever the lower fetters; I am incapable of doing so.
The Buddha addressed Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra. "Pūrṇa" is his surname;
in this language, it means "Full River."
Therefore, the *Puṇyavanta-sūtra* states:
Within the city of Rājagṛha, there was a brahmin couple who were very wealthy but had no children.
The two went to the banks of the Man River to seek out a shrine for Brahmādeva and beg for a son.
They offered various incense and flowers and recited divine mantras.
That night, the wife had a dream.
In a dream, she saw someone holding a vessel filled with precious objects and presenting it to her wife;
the wife immediately placed it before her abdomen,
and the vessel then entered her womb.
Having awakened, he recounted the dream.
His wife’s parents explained it for him, saying,
"This must surely be the Brahma King who has given you a son."
"If she gives birth, he shall become a vessel for jewels.
Consequently, she became pregnant;
after this child was born, he was intelligent and wise.
In debate, he was foremost in subduing non-Buddhists.
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, he recited and brought forth the Abhidharma-piṭaka.
Because he composed his work by the Mañjūṣa River, he was called Mañjuśrī (Mǎnjiāng).
Their names were also established based on their vows.
According to the *Adbhutadharmaparyāya-sūtra*, Pūrṇa,
out of a jealous heart, later severed his attachments and entered the mountains to recite ninety kinds of sūtras.
Having completed twenty-one years, he returned to Rājagṛha.
He set fire to his head and,
using copper razors, scraped his abdomen while proclaiming:
I am the Omniscient One; after me, another Buddha shall appear.
He then spoke this verse:
"If one has heard even a little and becomes arrogant, thereby conceited toward others..."
In this way, the blind man holding the torch illuminates others but cannot see himself.
Because of his wisdom, he threw himself to the ground and, before rising again, attained the fruit of arhatship. As for Maitrāyanīputra:
Mitrā is the name of the mother.
Within the four Vedas of the non-Buddhists, there is a chapter titled "Mitrā";
her mother recited this single chapter.
The name is derived from what she recites;
here it is called "Compassionate Practice" (Maitrīcārī), and also "Good Spiritual Friend" (Kalyāṇamitrī). *Ni* means "woman."
Since there are many who share the same name,
he is distinguished by his mother’s name.
Pūrṇa was rebuked because, despite being foremost in eloquence, he did not understand the dispositions of the faculties.
The *Vimala-sūtra* states:
"Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra. The four sections of the text are the same as before.
The third section first presents an inquiry and subsequently provides an explanation.
Within the explanation, there are four parts.

Second, the appearance of rebuking through the teaching;
third, from "entering samādhi" onwards, clarifying the skillfulness of his transformation;
fourth, from "I reflect" onwards, personally expressing his humility and submission.
At the beginning, he recalled how he had been rebuked in the past.

the place where he was rebuked was a grove near the city of Vaiśālī.

and the park contained monastic dwellings;

Regarding the exposition of the Dharma for newly ordained bhikṣus, this clarifies the matters censured.

At that time, Vimalakīrti came and said to me, etc.

within the preceding [section], there are four phrases;

Second, the reprimand;
third, the repeated instruction;
fourth, the repeated reprimand.
Regarding the statement, "First entering meditative concentration, one observes this person's mind and then preaches the Dharma":
"mind" refers to the mind of aspiration;

Because the mind has limitations and obstructions,
one sees [the object] while in meditative concentration,
but does not see it after emerging from concentration.
Even if one were in meditative concentration, a sharp-facultied śrāvaka would see that the faculties of sentient beings have matured only after eighty thousand kalpas;
for those of dull faculties, the concentration is shallow and slight, being insufficient to mention.
Therefore, he now instructs them.
First, one should enter meditative concentration to know the desires of people's minds,
and only then preach the Dharma.
For a Bodhisattva’s concentration, the true mind is the essence.
The nature is eternally quiescent and luminous, never failing to know;
it differs from the two vehicles in its manner of entering and emerging.
This is the second point of censure.
The lesser Dharma is like impure food, weeds, or tares;
the Great Mind is like nectar, comparable to a precious vessel.
This is the third stage of instruction.
Exhorting one to know the thoughts of the mind;
the fourth is a severe reprimand;
the lapis lazuli serves as a metaphor for the great mind.
This is great vaidūrya that illuminates and reflects all phenomena;
it is not like the ordinary vaidūrya found in this land.
The crystal is a metaphor for the Hīnayāna teachings.
In the second section concerning "not knowing the root," there are three phrases.
The first phrase censures not knowing the root;
the second phrase censures bestowing the minor [precepts].
The third phrase clarifies the harm of bestowing the Lesser Vehicle:
to preach the Lesser Vehicle to one destined for the Great Vehicle is feared to destroy their resolve for the Great Vehicle.
Therefore, do not cause harm.
Within the third section, which severely rebukes desire,
it does so by means of analogies.
Among these, there are three phrases:
the bhikṣu who seeks great fame desires to travel the Great Path;
minor dharmas are narrow and restricted, like a small footpath.
It is improper to seek the Great Teaching through the principles of the Small Vehicle;
therefore, it is said: "Do not show the small path.
One must not attempt to contain the great ocean within the footprint of an ox.
The great mind of a bhikṣu is like the great ocean;
minor dharmas, being slight and shallow, are comparable to the tracks of an ox.
To settle the mind and abide in the Dharma is designated as "internal."
This too should not be so, and thus it is said to be "non-existent.
As for the comparison of the sun's light to that of a firefly:
the bhikṣu’s great mind is like the light of the sun.
The dharmas of the Two Vehicles are minor matters, comparable to fireflies;
it is unreasonable to equate the Great with the small,
and thus they are said to be "incomparable."
If one follows the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa*,
there are two further lines:
"Do not attempt to equate Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains, with a mustard seed."
Furthermore, it is like a great lion’s roar being equated with the cry of a jackal.
In the fourth section, which provides a severe rebuke regarding the faculties, there are three sentences.
The first clarifies that although a bhikṣu has long since resolved upon the Great Mind, he has forgotten this intention.
This is because for those who have not yet realized the Dharma, progress and retreat are not constant.
Second, "How could the Small Vehicle... and so forth, rebukes that teaching by pointing out its many faults.
Third, "I observe the Small Vehicle... and so forth, rebukes it for failing to understand the faculties [of beings].
Their wisdom is shallow and slight, like that of a blind person;
their enlightened intelligence is inferior in substance.
Those of the Two Vehicles have only attained the wisdom of the emptiness of persons (pudgala-śūnyatā), but have not yet realized the emptiness of phenomena (dharma-śūnyatā).
Therefore, his wisdom was slight and shallow;
furthermore, he did not know the spiritual capacities of sentient beings, and for these reasons, it is said that his understanding was shallow.
Being unable to discern the sharpness or dullness of the various faculties,
their wisdom and function are narrow.
This clarifies that even Arhats are like blind men when it comes to the Mahāyāna Dharma.
How much more so for one such as I, a deluded ordinary person who gives rise to false discrimination?
Question:
The *Śrīmālā-sūtra* says:
Ordinary worldlings are like those born blind who do not see various forms;
Śrāvakas are like a seven-day-old infant who does not see the solar disk.
How can it now be said that Śrāvakas surpass those born blind?

Answer: Because ordinary worldlings (pṛthagjana) are unable to perceive the principle of the truths (satyadharma), that sutra says they are like those who are blind; whereas Śrāvakas have partially attained it.
It is said that a seven-day-old infant does not see the solar disk;
now it is said that because Śrāvakas do not recognize the nature of the faculties (indriya), they surpass even those born blind,
yet this does not mean they have seen the principle of the Truths (satyadharma).
Furthermore, it is said:
"In reality, the two vehicles do partially know the root-natures of sentient beings;
however, it is said that they are like the blind merely for the purpose of suppressing and discouraging the śrāvakas."
Therefore, the aforementioned sutra states:
"Pūrṇa, you should first enter meditative concentration to observe this person's mind, and only then preach the Dharma.
When it says that at that time Vimalakīrti entered samādhi, and so forth:
The following section is the third, which demonstrates his skillful transformation to lead [the audience] to realize that the Great supersedes the Small.
This passage consists of six sentences.
First: Vimalakīrti silently enters samādhi.
By entering into samādhi, this bhikṣu was enabled to recognize his own past lives;

he had previously planted roots of goodness and generated the aspiration for enlightenment in the presence of past Buddhas. This is based on the *Dharmadhātuvyāpya-śāstra* (Treatise on the Support of the Grounds).
There are five types of knowledge of past lives:
first, knowing one's own past lives;
second, knowing those of others.
Third, causing others to know;
fourth, causing others to know for themselves;
fifth, enabling oneself and others to mutually know their past lives.
What is being discussed here is precisely the fourth [power]: causing others to know their own past lives.
Question:
According to the Mahāyāna school, past phenomena do not exist as entities.
How does a bhikṣu come to know this? Answer:
By attaining the knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsajñāna*), he observes the seeds of the past within the present ālayavijñāna and thereby knows past events.
Alternatively,
it may be that one comes to know past events by perceiving the images reflected upon the mind.
Third, "Immediately, there was a sudden breakthrough," and below, he regained his original mind.

Through Vimalakīrti’s supernormal power of recollecting past lives, he empowered that bhikṣu so that he could see the roots of goodness he had cultivated in the past and recover his original Mahāyāna mind.
Fourth, having thus received such profound grace and paid his respects, the benefit he obtained was deep indeed.
Because their physical forms have vanished, it is called "ritual" (li).
Fifth, by means of these five causes, they are able to give rise to the aspiration for enlightenment and are further taught the Dharma.
Sixth, through this teaching of the Dharma, they no longer regress from Bodhi.
These bhikṣus were situated at the stage of the ten faiths;
by hearing this present teaching, they have entered the ten abidings and dwell in the non-retrogressive state within the seventh abiding.
Because they never regress to the two vehicles, it is not a non-regression of faith;
because they have long possessed faith, it is also not the non-regression of either realization or practice,
as they are still beginners.
Question:
Among the five kinds of bodhi, which bodhi do these bhikṣus realize? Answer:
Among these five, one merely realizes the bodhi of subduing the mind;
because one has long since had faith, this is not the arousal of the resolve (cittotpāda).
