the followers of external paths cultivate and attain the five supernatural powers (*pañcābhijñā*);
because these involve conceptual discrimination, they possess the characteristic of conditioned activity (*saṃskṛta-lakṣaṇa*).
If you now perceive objects as having the characteristic of form, you are no different from the non-Buddhists.
How, then, can they be called "internal"?
If there is no characteristic of activity, then within the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) dharmas, there is no characteristic of seeing.
"How can it be said again that he sees the three thousandfold world-system?
Since these points are both difficult to establish and difficult to reconcile,
the second [section] below describes how Nandika heard this and remained silent without answering.
The third [section] can be understood through the questions and praises of the various Brahmās.
In the fourth, Vimalakīrti explains that there is a Buddha, a World-Honored One, who has attained the true divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) by means of non-duality.
Zhuang said:
"The empty mind is eternally quiescent; although it universally conditions objects, there are no dualistic characteristics."
One does not perceive the characteristics of subject and object as distinct.
Thus, the *Sukhavihāra-sūtra* (Si-yi jing) states:
"Though one sees all classes of sentient beings throughout the realms of the ten directions, within the eye and its objects, one ultimately does not give rise to the duality of marks."
One is able to hear and receive all the teachings spoken by the Buddhas, yet within the sounds heard by the ear, one does not give rise to dualistic characteristics.
Furthermore, it is said that the divine eye of the two vehicles does not see while in meditative concentration, but sees immediately upon emerging from concentration.
Although one perceives the realms and grasps at signs through conceptualization, one is not yet able to see that which is beyond seeing.
The Tathāgata’s divine eye is equal in concentration and wisdom, yet it does not obstruct its illuminating function;
although he perceives the world, he does not engage in conceptual discrimination.
Why is this? Because one realizes that the nature of form is empty and perceives nothing to be seen;
thus, there is no differentiation between two distinct characteristics.
The meaning of the five eyes is briefly analyzed through seven gates:
first, the explanation of their names and how they are so designated;
second, the discernment of their essential nature.
Third, the sequence of cultivation and realization;
fourth, the distinctions among the five categories;
fifth, the differences in the objects perceived.
Sixth, distinguishing [the categories] by way of persons;
seventh, analyzing through questions and answers.
First, regarding the explanation of names and how they are derived:
First the general, then the specific.
Regarding the general:
"five" is the number.
The eye is itself its function.
It is called the "eye" because it illuminates and guides toward the objective realm before it;
this is a name derived from both its enumeration and its function.
This may be so; it is the "explanation by enumeration" (*saṃkhyā-vigraha*) among the six types of grammatical analysis.
Next, as for the specific [analysis]:
First is the fleshly eye (*māṃsa-cakṣus*).
When blood undergoes transformation and coagulates, it is termed "flesh.
Because the eye exists in dependence upon this flesh, it is called the fleshly eye.
The eye faculty is pure because it lacks blood and flesh;
since it is composed of the four great elements,
it derives its name from its physical basis.
Furthermore, some say that "flesh" is named after its own substance as the eye;
this interpretation is incorrect.
Second, the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*). There are two types of the divine eye:
first, that obtained through cultivation (*bhāvanā-labdha*); second, that obtained as a result of karmic retribution (*vipāka-labdha*).
Regarding those who have cultivated and attained the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*):
all meditative concentrations (*dhyāna-samādhi*) are termed "heaven" (*deva*).
Because the eye is obtained by relying upon heaven, it is called the "divine eye."
It is named after its basis.
Regarding the divine eye obtained as retribution,
there are two types of retribution.
First, concerning Bodhisattvas;
second, concerning the various devas.
Regarding those concerning Bodhisattvas:
The various bodhisattvas are called the Pure Gods (*śuddhāvāsa*).
Having been born among these gods, they have obtained the faculty of the eye as a karmic retribution;
it is from those Pure Gods that their name is established.
This is the eye of the Pure Heavens (Śuddhāvāsa), and is therefore called the "divine eye" (divyacakṣus);
it is named after its origin.
This is with respect to the various heavens.
All those in the celestial realms are radiant, pure, and bright;
they are therefore called "devas.
The eye of those in the celestial realm is called the "divine eye" (divyacakṣus).
It is named according to its destination.
Third is the eye of wisdom (*prajñā-cakṣus*).
Entering into principle through *prajñā* and investigating the truth of the principles is what is termed wisdom.
Taking wisdom as the eye is called the "eye of wisdom" (*prajñā-cakṣus*).
This is named after its essential nature. Alternatively, it may be understood as follows:
Among the six types of compound analysis, this is a *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound.
Fourth is the "Dharma-eye":
all phenomena (*dharma*) possess that which serves as a standard or support.
It may be acceptable to designate these as "dharmas. Alternatively,
the faculties, desires, dispositions, and so forth may be designated as "dharmas."
The eye that illuminates phenomena is called the Dharma-eye (*dharmacakṣus*);
it is named after its object.
There are five Buddha-eyes.
The four eyes mentioned previously continue through to the fruit of Buddhahood and are collectively termed the Buddha-eye;
this is precisely the eye of the Buddha-body.
It is named "Buddha-eye.
It is so called after its presiding deity; alternatively, it may be understood as follows.
"Buddha" has the meaning of "awakening.
Awakening is itself the eye;
it is called the Buddha-eye.
Taking the essence itself as the name is also acceptable. Furthermore,
that which illuminates and penetrates the Buddha-nature is called the Buddha-eye.
The designation is derived from its object.
Second, regarding the essential nature:
the fleshly eye has as its intrinsic nature the invisible, resistant pure matter produced by the four great elements of the human realm's pure faculties.
The three eyes—the eye of wisdom (*prajñā-cakṣus*), the Dharma-eye (*dharma-cakṣus*), and the Buddha-eye (*buddha-cakṣus*)—have as their essential nature that which arises from the mind.
The first is general, while the latter two are specific.
Regarding the general: all three eyes collectively take the mental factor of wisdom (*prajñā*) within the category of object-specific mental factors (*viṣaya-pratiniyata*) as their essential nature.
As for their distinction: the eye of wisdom has the fundamental non-conceptual knowledge (*mūla-jñāna*) as its nature;
the Dharma-eye has the subsequently attained knowledge (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*) as its nature. Alternatively, it may be understood thus:
The Dharma-eye (dharmacakṣus) has the wisdom of the true essence (samyaktva-jñāna) as its nature, because it takes the dharmas of ultimate truth as its object; thus it is called the "Dharma-eye.
If this is the case, how does it differ from the wisdom-eye (prajñā-cakṣus)?
The commentary states:
"The names by which they are designated differ;
wisdom itself constitutes the eye."
It receives its name from its essential nature;
it is called the "eye" for its illumination of phenomena;
it is designated according to its object.
The Buddha-eye has non-conceptual wisdom (*anābhoga-jñāna*) as its nature;
alternatively,
it may take the four wisdoms, such as the great perfect mirror wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*), as its essence.
Regarding the third [topic], the sequence of cultivation and accomplishment:
in order to guide and sustain the physical body, one first cultivates the fleshly eye (*māṃsa-cakṣus*).
Although it perceives coarse forms, it does not perceive subtle forms.
It sees what is near but not what is far;
it sees what is bright but not what is dark;
it sees what is before but not what is behind.
One sees what is within the obstruction but does not see what is beyond it;
there are many such obstructions. Next, one cultivates the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*).
Although one sees the realm of forms, one has not yet seen the true realm;
next, one cultivates the eye of wisdom.
Although one sees the true realm, one has not yet attained mastery over the conventional realm.
Next, one cultivates the Dharma-eye;
although it illuminates the four objects, it is not yet perfected.
Next, one cultivates the Buddha-eye.
Regarding the distinction between the fourth and fifth categories,
the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states:
"Of the five internal [bases], there are those produced by maturation (*vipākaja*) and those produced by cultivation (*aupacayika*), but none are produced by no-maturation (*avipākaja*)."
The eight unimpeded [knowledges] are both of the nature of outflow and of maturation;
the remaining three are substantially only dharmas;
and in terms of moments, they are only the latter three.
The two eyes of the fleshly devas have visible form as their nature;
they are of two types:
the first is that which is maturation (*vipāka*).
Because they arise from a ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*),
two [types of matter] are nurtured (*aupacayika*);
for they are benefited by superior conditions such as food, drink, sleep, and meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Having cultivated and attained the divine eye, it is not summoned by past karma,
but is induced solely through the power of meditative concentration;
it is merely a result of nourishment (*puṣṭi*) and not a ripened result (*vipāka*).
Apart from these two natures, there is no other outflowing result; therefore, it lacks the nature of an outflow.
Because it is not a patience toward suffering (*duḥkha-kṣānti*), it lacks momentariness.
Because it is not unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), it lacks substantial reality (*dravya*).

Regarding the eye of wisdom (*prajñā-cakṣus*): if considered in relation to the two vehicles (*śrāvaka-yāna* and *pratyekabuddha-yāna*), it possesses a momentary nature (*kṣaṇika*) because it is first attained at the stage of the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*).
If considered in relation to the Bodhisattva, it also possesses a momentary nature when it is first induced at the first stage (*prathamā bhūmiḥ*).
Because it is not indeterminate (avyākṛta), it lacks maturation (vipāka);
because it is not matter (rūpa), it lacks growth (aupacayika);
and because there was no prior outflow-free (anāsrava) state, it lacks outflow (naiṣyandika).
If one considers the seeds existing from the beginning, these also possess outflow (niṣyanda), for they are not unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) and thus lack substantiality.
The Dharma-eye arises from preceding untainted (anāsrava) states; therefore, it possesses outflow and is not indeterminate (avyākṛta).
Therefore, it has no maturation because it is not matter;
it has no nourishment because it does not arise at the beginning;
and it has no momentariness because it is unconditioned and lacks substantial reality.
The Buddha-eye consists of both the retributive and transformational eyes.
Because it arises from the previously attained outflow-free [wisdom], it possesses both outflow (niṣyanda) and nourishment (puṣṭi).
Since it is induced by the power of meditative concentration, the nature of the Buddha-eye belongs to the Dharma-body.
This [unconditioned] exists as a substantial entity;
the others are incomplete,
as has already been explained previously.
Fifth, regarding the differences in the objects perceived,
there are four points therein; first,
the object itself.
Second, phenomena;
third, principles;
fourth, realities.
The distinctions of the aggregates (skandha), elements (dhātu), and sense-bases (āyatana) are phenomena (vastu).
The various faculties, their natures, suffering, impermanence, and so forth are dharmas.
The suchness of the two emptinesses is the principle (tattva).
Within the Tathāgatagarbha, the true and eternal Buddha-nature is the reality.
These four dharmas are what the five eyes perceive;
the fleshly eye perceives only the single color of obstructed flesh, which is a mundane object.
Ordinary beings see one hundred yojanas with their physical eyes.
The physical eyes of those of the Two Vehicles see the same as what ordinary beings see.
The physical eyes of a Bodhisattva are as described in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
The farthest range of vision extends to the three thousandfold world system.
The Tathāgata’s physical eye is the same as that of a bodhisattva;
it perceives objects through differentiation.
The divine eye is of two kinds:
that obtained through karmic retribution and that obtained through cultivation.
These two types of the supernormal power of the divine eye perceive all material phenomena beyond obstructions.
Regarding those obtained through retribution, the objects perceived are indeterminate according to the strength or weakness of that retribution;
wherever the body resides, one perceives only the level of that specific ground and the lower levels, but not the higher levels.
Regarding those attained through cultivation:
according to the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*, the divine eye of an ordinary person perceives one four-continent world system (*cāturmahādvīpaka*).
As for the divine eye of a Śrāvaka, a lesser Śrāvaka perceives a small thousand-world system (*sāhasra-cūḍika-lokadhātu*).
The great śrāvakas see the intermediate chiliocosm;
because Aniruddha has cultivated excellence, he sees the trichiliocosm.
As for pratyekabuddhas, those with inferior divine eyes see the intermediate chiliocosm.
The superior [vision] sees the great trichiliocosm.
There are two types of the Bodhisattva’s divine eye: first, that obtained through cultivation; [second, that obtained through birth].
Second is that obtained through retribution.

As for that obtained through cultivation, what is seen varies according to the capacity of the individual; those with greater capacity see it as vast, while those with lesser capacity see it as small.
Those with far-reaching vision perceive all worlds.
Therefore, the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* states:
"A bodhisattva takes all worlds as the objective range of his divine eye. Regarding that which is obtained through retribution:
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states that while [the ordinary person] sees the trichiliocosm from an extreme distance,
the Tathāgata’s divine eye perceives all immeasurable worlds.
The latter three eyes cannot be discussed by means of expedient means;
they can only be distinguished according to the depth or shallowness of the Dharma.
The wisdom-eye of the two vehicles perceives only the emptiness of sentient beings.
The Bodhisattva’s eye of wisdom fully perceives the two kinds of emptiness,
yet does not exhaustively fathom them;
the Tathāgata’s eye of wisdom perceives emptiness to its ultimate limit.
The Dharma-eye of the Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha vehicles perceives only the general characteristics (sāmānya-lakṣaṇa) of phenomena, such as suffering and impermanence;
its coarse observation is unable to be subtle.
If one does not know the faculties and desires [of beings], then one lacks the Dharma-eye.

The Bodhisattva’s Dharma-eye perceives the faculties, dispositions, and natures of beings, as well as all phenomena—whether collectively or individually, whether coarse or subtle—knowing them all yet without reaching their ultimate limit.
The Tathāgata’s Dharma-eye is identical to that of the Bodhisattva, yet it reaches complete exhaustion; this is the Buddha-eye.
The two vehicles possess none at all;
among humans, bodhisattvas are uncertain as to whether they advance or retreat.
Bodhisattvas prior to the stages (bhūmi) possess both hearing and seeing.
Because buddha-nature is perceived through hearing and seeing, it does not yet possess the Buddha-eye.
Bodhisattvas on the stages see buddha-nature with their eyes;
because they see it with their eyes, it is said to exist.
According to the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*,
those from the ninth stage downward hear and see the Buddha-nature;
those at the tenth stage see it with their eyes, yet not clearly.
One merely perceives the Buddha-nature within oneself,
but does not perceive the Buddha-nature of sentient beings;
one sees but one-tenth of it within one's own person.
The Tathāgata’s Buddha-eye perceives the nature of reality to its ultimate limit;
this clarifies the vision of reality.
Sixth, the differentiation according to persons:
Initially, ordinary persons born among humans who have not yet abandoned desire possess only the fleshly eye (*māṃsa-cakṣus*).
However, if they cultivate and attain the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) of the higher realms, they acquire the divine eye (*divya-cakṣus*).
If one is born among the gods and has not yet abandoned desire, they possess only the fleshly eye (*māṃsa-cakṣus*);

those who have already abandoned desire, such as the gods of the desire realm, possess the divine eye (*divya-cakṣus*) obtained through karmic retribution (*vipākaja*), in addition to the fleshly eye.
There is the celestial eye obtained through retribution and the celestial eye obtained through cultivation.
Those born among the gods as a result of these two fruits possess the physical eye,
yet they have not yet attained the celestial eye obtained through retribution.
One does not attain the divine eye through the cultivation of fundamental dhyāna.
According to the *Mahāyānabuddhabhūmi-śāstra*,
the Srotāpanna and Sakṛdāgāmin fruits suppress the afflictions of the desire realm through contaminated wisdom.
Some attain the fundamental dhyānas and also cultivate the divine eye;
because they realize the emptiness of birth, they possess the wisdom eye;
yet, not knowing the faculties and desires, they lack the Dharma eye.
If one considers the knowledge of the dharmas of suffering and impermanence, it generally constitutes the *dharma-cakṣus*;
however, because it does not belong to a Buddha, it lacks the *buddha-cakṣus*.
If an *anāgāmin* is born among humans, they possess the *māṃsa-cakṣus*.
There is the eye attained through cultivation,
and there is the wisdom-eye.
If one is born among the devas, one attains the eye of divine retribution.
There are no other two eyes.
As previously understood, Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas possess the fleshly eye (*māṃsacakṣus*) and are endowed with both the karmic retribution eye and the cultivated divine eye (*divyacakṣus*).
Because one realizes the emptiness of sentient beings, there is the eye of wisdom;
there are no other two eyes.
This should be understood as previously explained.
Among those in the stage of a bodhisattva prior to the bhūmis, a bodhisattva who has attained sudden enlightenment possesses the fleshly eye, the divine eye, and the dharma-eye;
however, they have not yet attained the untainted [anāsrava] state and lack the wisdom-eye.
Because he is not yet a Buddha, he lacks the Buddha-eye.
From the first stage (*bhūmi*) up to the seventh stage, because he has not yet abandoned the body of segmented birth (*prādeśika-śarīra*), he possesses the fleshly eye;
because he cultivates meditative concentration (*samādhi*), he possesses the divine eye.
Because they have attained untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*), they possess both the Dharma-eye and the wisdom-eye;
this can be understood through the Buddha-eye.
If one reaches the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) or above, one possesses only three eyes.
Because they have abandoned the coarse分段 (*bhāgaśas*) [existence], they lack the fleshly eye (*māṃsa-cakṣus*);
because they are not yet Buddhas, they lack the Buddha-eye (*buddha-cakṣus*).

If these are bodhisattvas of the stage prior to the grounds (*bhūmi-pūrva*) who have turned their minds toward awakening through gradual realization, they possess the divine eye (*divya-cakṣus*), the wisdom-eye (*prajñā-cakṣus*), and the Dharma-eye (*dharma-cakṣus*).
Because they have already abandoned the coarse分段 (*paricchinna*) [existence], they lack the fleshly eye;
it is by means of the Buddha-eye that they can be known.
If those on the path of training (*śaikṣa*) turn their minds [toward the Mahāyāna], they possess all four eyes.
Because they have not yet abandoned the *pariccheda* (segmented existence), they possess the fleshly eye (*māṃsacakṣus*).
The remaining three eyes are as previously explained.
From the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) up to the tenth stage, they possess only three eyes.
What are called the divine eye, the wisdom eye,
and the dharma eye are to be known as non-dual when one reaches the stage of Buddhahood.
The three bodies possess [the eyes] either fully or partially.
The nirmāṇakāya possesses the five eyes;
the saṃbhogakāya possesses four eyes.
Because they lack the fleshly eye,
the dharma-body is true suchness;
it does not possess the five eyes.
If one considers the eye of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā-cakṣus*), it likewise possesses the five eyes.
Regarding the seventh question and answer for analysis:
Question:
Among the aggregates, elements, and bases, by what factors are the two eyes of the fleshly and divine types subsumed? Answer:
Both eyes have as their essence pure matter that is invisible and resistant.
This refers to the form-sphere (rūpadhātu), which is subsumed under the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha).
Question:
Within the gates of the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path, by what dharma is the "eye of wisdom" (prajñācakṣus) subsumed?
Answer:

It is subsumed under the eye of wisdom among the five faculties, the power of wisdom among the five powers, the factor of enlightenment of the investigation of phenomena among the seven factors of enlightenment, and right view among the eightfold noble path.
Question:
Among the three knowledges, four knowledges, or ten knowledges, by which of these dharmas is the Dharma-eye subsumed?
Answer: It is subsumed within the three knowledges, specifically within the two knowledges that enter into the subsequent attainment following the stage of preparatory application (*prayoga*).
The four knowledges that take conventional reality as their object all pertain to the four knowledges.

Among the ten knowledges, they are subsumed under five knowledges: conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), dharma knowledge (*dharmajñāna*), subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), path knowledge (*mārgajñāna*), and knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*).
Question:
Since the fleshly eye does not see beyond obstructions,
for what reason can it see the trichiliocosm?
Answer: A bodhisattva’s flesh eye, through the guidance and attainment of the divine eye, is able to see the trichiliocosm.
Because the flesh eye sees what is within obstructions while the divine eye guides it to see what is beyond obstructions.
The fleshly eye sees bright forms;
because it is guided by the divine eye, it sees dark forms. Answer:
There is the condition of light outside of obstructions;
because the divine eye guides it, one sees what is beyond obstructions.
In darkness, there is no condition of light.
Question: Although the divine eye (divyacakṣus) is induced [by meditative concentration], it cannot see [certain things], and so forth.
How do the five eyes and the ten eyes subsume one another? Answer:
According to the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, there are ten eyes.
The first is the flesh eye (*māṃsa-cakṣus*),
which sees all forms.
The second is the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*),
by which one sees all sentient beings dying here and being reborn there.
The third is the wisdom eye (*prajñācakṣus*).
To perceive the distinctions among all faculties is the Dharma-eye;
to perceive the true characteristics of all things is the Buddha-eye.
Fifth is the Buddha-eye,
which perceives the ten powers of the Buddha.
Sixth is the wisdom-eye, which discriminates.
To thoroughly know all aspects of phenomena is the seventh: the clear eye,
which means seeing the radiance of all Buddhas.
Eighth, the eye that emerges from birth and death,
because it perceives the dharma of nirvāṇa.
Ninth, the unimpeded eye.
Because they see all things without obstruction;
tenth is the Universal Eye,
which sees the dharma-gate of the equality of the dharma-realm.
Therefore, among the ten [powers], the first is the aforementioned fleshly eye (*māṃsa-cakṣus*), which also encompasses the divine eye (*divya-cakṣus*),
because seeing subtle objects at a distance or nearby constitutes the divine eye.
The second is the aforementioned divine eye.
The third is the eye of wisdom;
the fifth is the Buddha-eye;
the sixth is the eye of knowledge.
The seventh is the eye of clarity;
the eighth is the eye that transcends birth and death;
the ninth is the unimpeded eye.
These six eyes are as follows:
the aforementioned Dharma-eye is the fourth Dharma-eye;
because it perceives the ultimate truth, the aforementioned Wisdom-eye is the tenth Universal-eye.
This is because the Buddha-eye of the former [Buddha] universally perceives the equal and true Dharma-realm.

Therefore, when all the Brahmās of the fifth [heaven] resolve their minds, they hear that the Buddha-eye of the former [Buddha] is constantly luminous while in meditative concentration and does not give rise to discrimination; thus, they recognize what they themselves perceive.
Regarding those things that are not their proper portion, they all give rise to admiration and aspiration;
they exhaust themselves in diligent cultivation,
first generating the bodhicitta and subsequently initiating superior practices.
This, then, is the superior benefit of admonishing through instruction.
The sixth [point], reverential salutation, may be understood accordingly.
Thus, from "I have already" onwards, he concludes that [the opponent] is incapable [of practicing it].
The Buddha addressed Upāli;
in the correct phonetics of India,
this is translated as "Foremost" (Xiàngshǒu).
He was the most eminent among those who uphold the Vinaya.
Originally, when he was a layman, he was a barber for the Śākyas; later, when the Śākyas went forth from the household life, Upāli escorted them.
The Śākyas, wishing to go to where the Buddha was, removed their robes, jeweled crowns, and necklaces, and gave them along with the elephant they were riding to Upāli.
After the Śākyas had departed, Upāli reflected:
If even these sons of the Śākyas, despite such karmic retributions, still renounce their homes to become monks,
what benefit would there be for me to remain?
If they have attained [the goal], so should I.
I should do the same: place the goods I have obtained upon the tree and tie the elephant beneath it.
Having spoken these words,
"I shall give everything to all who take it," he later went to where the Buddha was.
When the Śākyas saw him, they asked about his purpose for coming;
Upāli answered them in full detail,
and the Śākyas were greatly delighted.
"Even if you invite the Buddha,
this man previously came to serve as my messenger;
if he later leaves the household life, I shall treat him with contempt."
"I pray that the Buddha will deliver me first, so that I may serve him with reverence.
The Buddha delivered him first and immediately conferred the precepts upon him.
When all the Śākyas likewise paid their respects, at that moment the great earth shook.
A voice from the sky praised him, saying:
"Among all the sons of the Śākyas, my mountain of pride has collapsed;
since his renunciation, he has been foremost in upholding the Vinaya."
They are rebuked because they are unable to contemplate emptiness to extinguish their transgressions.
As for the meaning of "practicing," it has already been explained as before.
Since the assembly collectively adheres to it, it must be commanded.
The four textual divisions are the same as before.
In the third section, the commentary first presents a general inquiry, second provides a detailed explanation, and finally offers a concluding summary.
Within this main text, five sections are opened.
First, the matter of being rebuked in the past is mentioned;
second, from "At that time, Vimalakīrti" onwards, the manner of the reprimand is clarified;
third, from "Then the two bhikṣus said" to "O, how wise!", the praise offered by the two bhikṣus for Vimalakīrti is manifested.
Fourth, my response below clarifies the subsequent praise.
Fifth, the passage beginning "At that time, the two bhikṣus' doubts and regrets were immediately removed" clarifies how the bhikṣus gained benefit upon hearing the Dharma.

Within the former [section], it is recorded: "I recall that in the past there were two bhikṣus who had violated the disciplinary rules; feeling ashamed, they did not dare to ask the Buddha, but came instead to question me."
This is the first matter of censure.
It consists of two parts:
first the question, and subsequently the answer.
In this first question,
it is clarified that because the bhikṣu’s sense of shame and remorse regarding his transgression was so profound, he did not dare to ask the Buddha;
instead, he came to Upāli to seek a definitive resolution, as Upāli was foremost in the mastery of the Vinaya.
Not knowing the relative weight [of the offenses], he sought to resolve his original doubt.
The Vinaya states: "There was a bhikṣu."
While he was sleeping in an araṇya,
a wood-gathering woman saw him,
and her lustful desire arose intensely.
She committed an act of theft and unrighteousness.

Unlike other bodhisattvas, the leftovers of what he has eaten cannot be exhausted; this clearly demonstrates that the Buddha’s physical body and its retributive function are inexhaustible.

Herein, in the fourth section, it is correctly clarified that his enjoyment is inexhaustible. Within the second part concerning the excellence of the food, three aspects of the merit of eating are revealed.
First, regarding the explanation of physical well-being (*kāya-prasrabdhi*):
freedom from forgetfulness and unwholesomeness is called "peace" (*praśama*);
being free from suffering and experiencing serenity is called "bliss" (*sukha*).
For example, the subsequent section uses a simile to manifest peace and bliss.
Later, when it clarifies that the bodies of those who eat [the food] emit a wondrous fragrance, this also uses the preceding simile to manifest the characteristics of that fragrance.
From the passage beginning with "At that time, Vimalakīrti questioned the assembly regarding the Fragrant [Buddha-land]" onwards...
The third major section clarifies that his teaching is distinct and extraordinary;
herein there are two parts.
First, it clarifies the Buddhas of other [realms].
The latter part clarifies the Buddhism of this land.
Within the former [part], there are two sections.
First is the inquiry of Vimalakīrti.
Next, that bodhisattva replied:
"Speaking according to reason,
the teachings are in truth not distinct."
It is simply because the retributive faculties and natures of sentient beings differ that they ask this question.
Within the preceding section, he first asks about that [land], and [the Buddha] answers it in full:
"In my land, the Tathāgata has no teaching through words and letters; rather, practitioners enter the discipline solely through various fragrances."
It is not that the land is silent and without speech that it is called "without verbal expression.

Rather, it is because the manner in which the sages bring about transformation differs from that of the sentient beings in this land—where they must attain the Way through verbal instruction—whereas in that country, most devas and humans enter the ranks of the noble ones primarily by smelling fragrances.
The subsequent scripture states:
"Or they may perform the Buddha-work by means of fragrant food," and so forth.
When it says there are no verbal explanations, it merely cites the most prominent examples.
That country takes the "path of fragrance" as its fundamental principle;
it is not that speech is entirely absent there.
Therefore, the aforementioned sutra says:
In that land, there are no names for śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas;
there is only a multitude of bodhisattvas,
for whom the Buddha preaches the Dharma.
Thus we know that there are also verbal teachings;
just as in this land one may attain awakening through the opening of the Way, or by means of miraculous transformations and other such events.
As for the Samādhi of the Treasury of Virtue (Guṇagañja-samādhi):
The Sage achieves this through meditative concentration;
having attained this concentration, all the merits of a bodhisattva are fully perfected.
Therefore, it is called the "Treasury of Virtues Samādhi."
From here below is the second section, which clarifies how that bodhisattva inquires about the teachings regarding this land and how they are bestowed as a transformative instruction.
Within this, there is first the question and then the answer.
The answer consists of three parts.
First, a general statement by way of introduction;
second, a detailed explanation beginning with "The second is hell";
third, the conclusion.
The sentient beings of this land are stubborn and difficult to transform; therefore, for them, he speaks words suited to their stubbornness.
Yet, the Sage’s transformation of others is without fixed method, responding according to conditions.
Because the sentient beings of this land are stubborn and difficult to transform, the Buddha responds to them with coarse speech.
The Buddha has three ways of teaching the Dharma.
The first is teaching with gentle words regarding the joyful fruits of practicing virtue.
Second, harsh speech, which results in the fruit of suffering from evil conduct;
third, frivolous speech.
Sometimes they rebuke them with harsh words,
and sometimes they transform them with gentle speech;
only by employing these two methods in combination can one truly abandon faults.
Among the three teachings, this is the coarse teaching.
Within the second, the distinct [teaching], there are three parts:
first, the Dharma.
Second, the analogies;
third, the application.
Within the Dharma, this is explained by way of the Four Noble Truths.
It must be clarified because one wishes to lead sentient beings to realize that the Lesser Vehicle is ultimately wearying and that they should ultimately pursue the Mahāyāna.

Within the initial clarification of the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*), it first explains the most grievous sufferings of the three miserable realms (*apāya*) to terrify those sentient beings and cause them to abandon evil causes.
These "places of difficulty" refer to the eight difficulties (*aṣṭāv akṣaṇāḥ*).
Among these, the three evil destinies and the four factors of being born blind or deaf constitute the "difficulties of retribution.
They have as their essence the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) that are of the nature of maturation and indeterminate (*vipāka-avyākṛta*).
Worldly wisdom and eloquence are afflictions that are difficult to overcome,
for they take defiled, perverse discernment as their essence.
In the northern continent of Uttarakuru, where there is longevity, these two do not exist.
This place is difficult [to attain],
for it is difficult for the world-system where one dwells to be formed;
its substance consists of the four great elements.
Because those devas and humans possess complete faculties and their natures are sharp and wise, it is not difficult for them; however, because they reside there, it may also be considered difficult.
Thus, both the body and the location constitute difficulties.
It takes as its essence the five aggregates (skandhas) that are resultant and indeterminate (vipāka-avyākṛta).
This is difficult to reconcile with the Buddha’s earlier and later statements,
because when the body falls into this state, it likewise takes as its essence the five aggregates that are resultant and indeterminate.
To possess the aforementioned eight factors and yet fail to attain the noble path or the means to the noble path is called "difficult.
This refers to the birthplace of such deluded persons.
This refers to those remote borderlands where heterodox practitioners with wrong views reside and where the Three Jewels are absent.
Following the section on the body and its perversions, the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*) is now clarified.
Although within this text there is both cause and effect, [the focus here is on the cause].
This collectively cites the results to explain their causes,
intending to clarify the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*).
It means that bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, and mental misconduct [are the causes].
This clarifies the three types of action (*karma*).
The accumulation of form and shape is called the body (*kāya*).
Based on the body, one initiates actions that are improper and contrary to principle; these are termed wrong conduct (*mithyācāra*).
The other two are likewise so;
they both have universal volition (*cetanā*) as their essential nature.
If categorized by way of predominance:
According to the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*, there are three types of volition (*cetanā*):
first, deliberative volition;
second, determinative volition.
Third, the volition that initiates action:
the seven types of bodily and vocal karma take the thorough determination of the place of action as their preparatory stage (*prayoga*),
and take the volition that initiates action as their essential nature (*svabhāva*).
Regarding the three types of mental karma,
they take the two kinds of volition— deliberative and decisive— as their essence.
Therefore, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:

The two types of volition (*cetanā*) that have reached the stage of definitive decision are associated with mental activity; because they cause the mind to move, they are called "mental karma" (*manas-karman*).
Following the section on killing, the ten non-virtuous actions (*daśākuśala*) are next explained.
The act of severing life is termed "killing."
That is the very body;
by using it to produce that prior object,
one kills those sentient beings.
This is naming it according to its function and its object.
However, for the killing of a sentient being, five conditions must be fulfilled.
The first is that the victim must be reckoned as a sentient being.
Second is the intention,
which refers to the arising of a harmful mind.
Third is the expedient means.
Because desire is harmful, one must grasp swords and staves.
Fourth are the afflictions,
namely greed, hatred, and delusion.
Fifth is completion.
This means that those sentient beings die either immediately or at a later time;
if these five conditions are met, it constitutes a fundamental course of action (*maula-karmapatha*).
If even one condition is missing, it constitutes a preparatory act (*prayoga-karma-patha*).
Regarding the retribution for killing,
the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states:
There are three types of results produced by unwholesome karma:
first, the ripened result (*vipākaphala*).
According to whether the karma is inferior, middling, or superior, one experiences the ripened results of rebirth as an animal, a hungry ghost, or in hell.
Second is the flow-on fruit (niṣyanda-phala):
subsequently obtaining a human body with a short lifespan.
Third is the sovereign fruit (adhipati-phala).
One perceives external objects as lacking luster; this is because,
by killing others and causing them to suffer, one undergoes the ripening fruit (vipāka-phala) in hell.
Because one has taken the life of another, one receives a short lifespan among human beings as the result of uniform outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*).
Because one has destroyed the power of others, one experiences external objects as lacking luster.
This refers to the dominant fruit (*adhipati-phala*).
Regarding "taking what is not given is the retribution for taking what is not given":
that which belongs to another and has not yet been bestowed is called "not given."
Regarding this, I privately remark:
"Taking" refers to the function of this body;
thus, it is named according to its function and its object.
There are three types of retribution:
one undergoes the ripening fruit (*vipākaphala*) within the hells;
having emerged from there, one is born among humans with meager wealth and resources.
These are the outflowing fruits (niṣyanda-phala).
That external objects frequently suffer from frost and hail is the dominant fruit (adhipati-phala).
Regarding "sexual misconduct" and the retribution for sexual misconduct:
that which deviates from proper decorum is called sexual misconduct;
this is also named after its practice.
Furthermore, one experiences three fruits of retribution:
receiving the ripening fruit (*vipākaphala*) within the three evil destinies;
and, when born in the human realm, having an unfaithful wife.
It produces the fruit of outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*),
whereby the external world is replete with many impurities;
this is the sovereign fruit (*adhipati-phala*).
Regarding this false speech and its retribution:
speaking words that are not true is called false speech.
This, too, is named according to its function.
One obtains three kinds of fruits:
one undergoes the fruit of maturation (vipākaphala) in the hells and other realms;
if born among humans, one is frequently subjected to slander.
It receives the fruit of outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*);
externally, it brings about material requisites that are largely foul and impure.
This is the fruit of increase (*adhipati-phala*).
Regarding this retribution for divisive speech (*paiśunya*):
creating separation between this person and that person is what is called divisive speech.
This, too, is named according to its function.
Furthermore, one experiences three results:
receiving the ripening fruit (*vipākaphala*) within the evil destinies;
and subsequently, being born among humans with the alienation of kinsmen and friends.
It receives the fruit of outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*).
That which brings about external objects that are high and low, precipitous and crooked,
is the sovereign fruit (*adhipati-phala*).
Regarding "harsh speech" and its retribution for harsh speech:
uttering words that are coarse and evil is called harsh speech.
This, too, is named according to its function.
There are three ways in which the fruit is experienced:
first, one undergoes the ripening fruit (*vipākaphala*) within the lower miserable realms;
subsequently, when born into the human path, one constantly hears evil sounds.
One experiences the fruit of uniform outflow (niṣyanda-phala).
As for the perception of a world of fields abounding in thorns,
being stony and saline— this is the sovereign fruit (adhipati-phala).
Regarding "meaningless speech" and the retribution for meaningless speech:
that which does not accord with the correct meaning is called "meaningless speech.
This, too, is designated by name according to its function.
They further experience three fruits:
they undergo the ripening fruit (*vipākaphala*) within the three evil destinies;
subsequently, when born among humans, their speech lacks majesty and authority.
It receives the fruit of uniform outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*).
That it brings about changes in the seasons of the external world is the dominant fruit (*adhipati-phala*).
Regarding "this poverty, envy, and the retribution of envy":
being stained by many objects of attachment is called poverty and envy;
as for its retribution, it results in three fruits.
One experiences the ripening fruit (*vipākaphala*) in the three evil realms, such as the animal realm;
within the human realm, one experiences the concordant fruit (*niṣyandaphala*) through a mind characterized by greed for power and so forth,
resulting in the external world having meager fruits.
This is the dominant fruit (*adhipati-phala*).
Regarding "the retribution of anger and affliction":
causing damage to objects within one's environment is termed "anger and affliction."
The fruition of the result is also threefold:
one undergoes the ripening fruit (*vipākaphala*) in the lower evil destinies;
when among the human realm, one's mind is fierce and intense, constantly full of anger and resentment.
One experiences the fruit of uniform outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*).
That external worldly fruits are bitter or pungent in taste is the sovereign fruit (*adhipati-phala*).
Regarding the fruit of wrong view and the retribution for wrong view:
giving rise to incorrect views is called "wrong view," and it likewise yields three fruits.
Experiencing the ripening fruit (*vipākaphala*) in the three evil destinies,
one is subsequently born among humans with an increased mind of delusion and many wrong views;
this is the concordant fruit (*niṣyandaphala*).
The fact that one perceives the external world as lacking all fruits is the sovereign fruit (*adhipatiphala*).
Following this discussion on stinginess, the text next clarifies the six obscurations (*āvaraṇa*).
Regarding the retribution for stinginess:
stinginess is itself a fetter of avarice; by obstructing the giving of others, one undergoes the ripened fruit of maturation in the lower miserable realms.
In a future birth among humans, one receives the retribution of poverty due to a lack of wealth and resources;
this is the fruit of uniform outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*). The dominant fruit (*adhipati-phala*) is as previously described.
Regarding the retribution for violating the precepts:
because of such transgressions, one is born into the three evil realms and undergoes the ripening fruit (vipāka-phala);
subsequently, even when born among humans, one constantly and frequently violates the precepts.
These are the results of outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*).
As for the retribution of hatred,
one undergoes the ripened fruit (*vipāka-phala*) in the lower miserable realms.
To be born among humans and receive the retribution of ugliness as well as excessive anger is the fruit of uniform outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*).
This is the retribution for laziness.
Due to indolence, one receives a body in the miserable realms;
this is the fruit of maturation (vipākaphala).
In subsequent births among humans, their nature will be largely characterized by indolence.
These are the results of outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*). Regarding the retribution for a distracted mind:
due to mental distraction, one is born in the three evil destinies and undergoes the fruit of maturation (*vipāka-phala*).
Being born in the human realm with a mind characterized by much distraction is the result of outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*).
It may also be understood as the dominant result (*adhipati-phala*).
Following the section on the establishment of the precepts, this next portion clarifies the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*).
Although the text generally cites both the false and the correct,
it is explained here next because the intention is to distinguish the correct by contrasting it with the false.
In this text, the meaning is elucidated by way of the three trainings:
first, ethical discipline;
second, meditative concentration.
Regarding the subsequent benefit:
as for those who establish the precepts,
it is because sentient beings have previously committed evil that the Buddha establishes the precepts for them, so that they may cultivate goodness.
Regarding those who uphold the precepts and those who violate them:
since the establishment of the precepts,
to follow the teachings is called "upholding."
To violate them is called "transgression.
Alternatively, it may be said that maintaining them is called "observance through restraint."
The name "transgression" refers to ceasing [from non-transgression]. Zhuang said:
"To give rise to thoughts and stir up mental activity is what is called a transgression."
Not grasping at their characteristics is called upholding the precepts.
Thus, the *Dharmapada* says: "Regarding the various ways of upholding the precepts..."
There is neither good nor the nature of the precepts of dignified conduct, which are like empty space.
To uphold them is to be deluded and inverted.
That which is to be performed is itself the upholding.
To do what should not be done constitutes an offense.
Regarding "this is an obstacle":
these two preceding offenses are able to obstruct the Noble Path.
Regarding "non-obstruction":
these two aforementioned types of upholding do not obstruct the Noble Path.
Regarding "incurring offense": [this refers to the opposite].
Regarding the two preceding offenses,
these are miscellaneous transgressions; regarding the two preceding observances, these are [meritorious] restraints.
Regarding this "purifying the defilements," the following section clarifies the training in concentration (*samādhi-śikṣā*).
As the vernacular proverb says:
Right concentration is called "purity," while wrong concentration is termed "defilement. Yuan said:
Pure concentration and untainted concentration are "pure";
concentration associated with relishing is called "defiled.
This is also acceptable.
"Purity" refers to untainted concentration (*anāsrava-samādhi*);
"defilement" refers to all mundane concentrations (*laukika-samādhi*).
It is also said:
To differentiate between these two characteristics is called defilement;
not grasping at these two characteristics is called pure concentration (*śuddha-samādhi*). Regarding "outflows" (*āsrava*) and "without outflows" (*anāsrava*):
Next, the training in wisdom is explained.
That which is with outflows consists of the three outflows;
that which is without outflows excludes the three outflows.
It may be that the preparatory knowledge (*prayoga-jñāna*) prior to the stages (*bhūmi*) is understood as being with outflows (*sāsrava*),
whereas the two types of knowledge— the fundamental (*mūla*) and the subsequently attained (*pṛṣṭhalabdha*)— on the stages themselves are without outflows (*anāsrava*).
Alternatively,
according to the Abhidharma-śāstra,
there are six meanings.
First, because of the intrinsic nature of the outflows;
second, because of their mutual association with the outflows;
third, because they are bound by the outflows.
Because they are accompanied by the four outflows;
because they are conducive to the five outflows;
and because they are of the same nature as the six outflows.
Regarding the self-nature of the outflows (*āsrava*):
it is called "with outflows" (*sāsrava*) because the various outflows are conjoined with the nature of being an outflow.
Regarding the association of the outflows:
This means that mental states and other phenomena co-arising with the outflows (āsrava) are called "with outflows" (sāsrava) because they are associated with the outflows and serve as their basis.
As for those "bound by the outflows," this refers to wholesome phenomena with outflows, which, through the power of the outflows, bring about future existence.
"Accompanied by outflows" means that the dharmas of other stages are likewise pursued and followed by the heavy outflows belonging to those other stages.
"Conducive to outflows" means...
This means that the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) are accompanied by the heaviness of various afflictions (*kleśa*).
As for "belonging to the category of outflows" (*āsravapakṣya*),
it refers to the fact that the contaminated aggregates (*sāsrava-skandha*) of an Arhat are produced by the afflictions of their previous lives.
That which possesses the six aforementioned characteristics is termed "with outflows" (sāsrava).
That which is contrary to these is termed "without outflows" (anāsrava).
As for the "wrong path" and the "right path":
The practices of the non-Buddhists are called "false," while those cultivated by the followers of the Inner Way are called "correct.
This is also acceptable.
The practice of the two vehicles is called "deviant," while the practice of the bodhisattva is called "correct. Alternatively, it may be understood as follows:
To grasp at the characteristics of the heterodox and the orthodox is called heterodoxy;
not seeing heterodoxy or orthodoxy is called orthodoxy.
As for the conditioned and the unconditioned:
Next, the Truth of Cessation is explained.
In this text, both the incorrect and the correct are mentioned together;
the intention is to clarify what is correct by contrasting it with what is incorrect.

The two types of contaminated (*sāsrava*) five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*)— those subject to disintegration and transformation— which are produced by karma and afflictions (*kleśa*) and altered by the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*),

are called "conditioned" (*saṃskṛta*). Alternatively, the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) five aggregates, which are subject to the flux of the four characteristics such as arising (*jāti*) and so forth, are also termed "conditioned."
That which is eternally extinguished within the causal state is called the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Alternatively,
the two types of cause and effect— those of fragmented [rebirth] and those of transformation— are called the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
Because it is the ultimate exhaustion and eternal cessation, it is termed "unconditioned" (*asaṃskṛta*).
However, there are many types of this unconditioned;
according to the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya*, the *Abhidharmakośa*, the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, and other texts, there are three kinds.
1. Space; 2. Cessation through deliberation;
3. Cessation not through deliberation.
Based on the *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-ṭīkā* (Pal-zhen-lun) and the *Pañcaskandhaka*, four unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) are established:
first, space (*ākāśa*); second, cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Third is non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha),
and fourth is suchness (tathatā).
According to the *Śata-dharma-śāstra* and the Vijñaptimātra school, six unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta) are established.
1. Space; 2. Cessation through deliberation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha); 3. Cessation not through deliberation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha).
Fourth, the immovables;
fifth, the cessation of perception and feeling; sixth, suchness.
Based on treatises such as the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and the *Abhidharma-samuccaya*, eight unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) are established.
Five types are as previously mentioned;
to these are added the true nature (*tathatā*) of wholesome phenomena, the true nature of unwholesome phenomena, and the true nature of indeterminate phenomena, making eight kinds in total.
Question:
Why do the various treatises differ? Answer:

In the *Abhidharmakośa* and the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*, the "one hundred dharmas" as mere consciousness (*vijñaptimātra*) establish six types of unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) by dividing cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) into "immovability" (*āniñjya*) and the "cessation of perception and feeling" (*saṃjñā-vedita-nirodha*).

In the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and the *Abhidharma-samuccaya*, following treatises such as the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*, they establish eight types of unconditioned phenomena based on the three abodes (*tri-vihāra*) of true thusness (*tathatā*).
These masters differ in their interpretations regarding the meaning [of the categories], resulting in various ways of opening and closing them;
yet there is no contradiction in principle.
Herein, the six unconditioned phenomena are explained according to the Vijñaptimātra (Consciousness-Only) perspective.
Briefly, there are two types.
First, based on the transformation of consciousness;
that is, having previously heard it taught that there are six unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*).
Due to the power of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), when consciousness arises, its objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*) manifests;
this is actually conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
Because it remains unchanged and is similar from one moment to the next, it is conventionally designated as "unconditioned" (*asaṃskṛta*).
Second, six types are provisionally established based on the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
The first is the *tathatā* of space:
because it is free from the obstruction of form, it is conventionally designated as "space."
The second is cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), which is suchness (*tathatā*):
based on the above, by means of wisdom’s discernment one abandons the afflictions and realizes suchness, which is conventionally designated as "cessation through deliberation.
The third is non-deliberative cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
There are two kinds. The first is the fundamental nature (*prakṛti*).
This refers to the true thusness (*tathatā*), which is by nature free from defilement; it is conventionally designated as "non-analytical" (*apratisaṃkhyā*) [cessation].
The second is the deficiency of conditions (*pratyaya-vaikalya*).

This refers to the fact that when the conditions for the arising of tainted (*sāsrava*) or untainted (*anāsrava*) phenomena upon the *tathatā* (suchness) are deficient, they do not arise; this is conventionally designated as "non-analytical cessation" (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
There are two types of non-arising.
First, never-arising;
second, temporary non-arising;
fourth, immovability.
That is to say, based on the true thusness (tathatā), the cessation of feelings of suffering and pleasure is metaphorically designated as "immovability" (āniñjya).
Fifth is the cessation of perception and feeling (saṃjñāvedayitanirodha);
that is to say, based on the true thusness, the cessation of perception and feeling is metaphorically designated as the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta).
The sixth is *tathatā* (suchness).
It is established, designated, and provisionally taught as suchness by way of that which is revealed through the two kinds of emptiness—of persons and phenomena.
The reason for this is as follows:

Because the essence of *tathatā* (suchness) is not an established truth (*prajñaptisatya*), it is free from the characteristics of names and language and is realized solely through direct, essential realization (*sākṣātkāra*).
Question:
Among the three or two types of unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), such as the immovable (*āniñjya*), under which unconditioned phenomenon is this subsumed?
Answer: According to the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*,
if it is a temporary cessation, it is subsumed under non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Ultimate cessation is subsumed under analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Regarding "worldly nirvāṇa":
the causes and effects of birth and death are termed the "world."
Because it is subject to destruction, the cessation within the fruit is termed *nirvāṇa*.
However, there are four distinct types of *nirvāṇa*:
first, that which is intrinsically pure and not defiled by afflictions.
It has the stained *tathatā* (suchness) as its essence.
Second, non-abiding compassion and wisdom do not dwell in either extreme;
through the realization of *nirvāṇa*, one immediately becomes free from the cognitive obstacles (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
Its essence is the true suchness (*tathatā*) of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmas*).
Although the three remaining obstacles have been eternally stilled, as long as the body has not yet been relinquished,
one realizes nirvana through the body.
It takes the true suchness (tathatā) of the severed afflictive hindrances as its essence.
It is "without remainder" because it has abandoned both sufferings of birth-and-death; this is what is called "without remainder."
That is, one immediately transcends birth and death if the true suchness (tathatā) constitutes the essence.
Furthermore, it says:
"The first [of the three bodies] is precisely true suchness."
The latter three are subsumed under cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). There are two kinds of cessation:
first, the attainment of cessation through the severance of bonds.
This refers to the analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) obtained through the afflictive hindrances (kleśāvaraṇa). Second is the attainment through the hindrance of cessation;
this refers to the analytical cessation obtained through the cognitive hindrances (jñeyāvaraṇa).

The cessation with remainder (sopadhiśeṣa-nirodha) has the analytical cessation of the destruction of bonds as its essence; the cessation without remainder (nirupadhiśeṣa-nirodha) has the analytical cessation of the obstruction to dwelling [in saṃsāra] as its essence.
Alternatively, it may be so.
Nirvana by nature has non-analytical cessation as its essence,
