This is illustrated by the analogy of a medicine that purges, which serves to clarify the name [of the food].
It is said: "Regarding 'superior flavor,' this enumerates the names of medicinal herbs;
those that possess manifest medicinal efficacy beneath [the surface] are suitable for such rice."
The superior flavor eliminates the inferior combination;
once all the poisons within the body have been eliminated, it is then digested.
Question:
Since fragrant food is a material phenomenon (*rūpadharma*),
how can it sever the afflictions? Answer:
Yuan said:
"It is by the inconceivable power of the fragrant food of great compassion that one is able to sever the afflictions (*kleśa*).
It is like the wheel-turning monarch (*cakravartin*) who possesses a precious couch."
When the sage-king occupies the highest position,
he is able to transcend desire and attain the four kinds of jade maidens.
Even when seeing them, it is like beholding a Buddha image;
one does not give rise to lustful thoughts,
much less regarding the sensory realms experienced by Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
As it is said in the sutra:
"A bodhisattva possesses a crown that illuminates the nature of phenomena (dharmatā).
When he wears this and contemplates, all dharmas appear before his mind."
All matters are likewise.
Although this interpretation exists,
it is not logically tenable.
How could it be that the nature of material phenomena (*rūpadharma*) is capable of severing delusions?
It is only by means of fragrant food that one’s power of insight (*vipaśyanā-jñāna*) is nurtured and stimulated so as to sever afflictions;
it is not the substance of the food itself that can sever delusions.
The third category reveals that all things constitute the Buddha-work.
This section contains three parts:
first, Ānanda’s praise of the Tathāgata and his confirmation of the teaching.
Second, the Buddha’s activities are explained in detail by way of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
Third, the section concludes with a summary.
First, Ānanda offers praise.
Rice is fundamentally for filling the void and sustaining physical strength;
that it should now sever delusions and attain the Way—
is this not truly unprecedented?
Regarding the Tathāgata’s seal of approval (*anumodanā*):
because that which is praised accords with reason, he seals it by saying, "It is so" (*evam etat*).
Second, in the extensive explanation of the Buddha-activities, there are fifteen phrases within the text.
The meaning is divided into two parts:
the first fourteen phrases concern the performance of Buddha-activities in accordance with the flow [of samsara],
while the final one phrase concerns the performance of Buddha-activities against the flow.
The preceding section is further divided into two parts:
the first thirteen phrases specifically clarify the Buddha’s activities,
while the final phrase generally clarifies the Buddha’s activities.
At the beginning or in the middle [of the teaching], there may be certain buddha-fields where the Buddha’s light constitutes the Buddha-work.
In such cases, the visual consciousness itself can serve as the Buddha-work by taking the sensory objects of form as its medium;
through beholding the Buddha’s light, one awakens to the Noble Path.
Therefore, it is called "Buddha-work.
Thus, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"Those who encounter this light have all their afflictions completely eliminated."
Regarding those bodhisattvas who become buddhas:
as in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*,
the World-Honored One remains silent while causing the bodhisattvas to preach the Dharma and deliver sentient beings, thereby performing the work of a buddha.
Regarding "the Buddha transforms people":
the Buddha manifests as a human being and preaches the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings so that they may attain enlightenment.
These two preceding phrases indicate that the faculty of auditory consciousness can serve as a conduit for the sound-object to perform the work of a Buddha.
There are those for whom the Bodhi tree performs the work of a Buddha.
Because the Buddha attained enlightenment beneath such a tree, it is called the Bodhi tree.
This tree possesses exquisite color and fragrance, and it further emits various perfumes.
Seeing, hearing, smelling, and knowing all lead to the realization of the Holy Path;
this is precisely how the five consciousnesses can take the five sense objects as the Buddha’s work.
[This applies to] clothing, bedding, and requisites.
In the past, the King of Jambudvīpa obtained a Buddha’s *kāṣāya* robe and suspended it upon a tall banner to show it to the people of the country.
Those who were ill, upon seeing it, took refuge in it;
their illnesses were all cured.
To give rise to the bodhicitta and,
by means of this, awaken to the Way is what is called "Buddha-work."
This means that visual consciousness can take the object of form as a Buddha-work.

As for "with fragrant food," because one partakes of fragrant food, one attains entry into the Noble Path; this means that the [other] three consciousnesses can take the three objects as Buddha-works.
The meaning of the four nutriments (*āhāra*) is analyzed through six sections:
first, the explanation of their names and how they are designated;
second, the determination of their essential nature (*svabhāva*).
The establishment of the three types of higher knowledge (trividyā), the distinctions among the four analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid),
and the existence or non-existence of the realms (dhātu) and destinies (gati).
The six questions and answers are briefly summarized here.
First, regarding the explanation of the name and how it is derived, there are two types:
first, the general, and second, the specific.
Regarding "initially penetrating":
"four" refers to the number;
"food" refers to its function.
It is named according to its number and its function;
alternatively, it may be understood as the *dvigu* (numeral-determinative) compound among the six types of grammatical analysis (*ṣaṭ-vibhakti*).
Regarding the two specific names:
first is "cutting off food.
"Cutting off" refers to the cutting off of form; that is, it is a formal characteristic.
Food refers to that which nourishes the sense faculties and the primary elements;
this is designated by way of its form and its function. Alternatively, it may be understood as follows:
Cessation is itself the food of the Buddha;
it receives its name from its essential nature.
Second is the food of contact (*sparśāhāra*).
Contacting an object before one is termed "contact" (sparśa).
Because it benefits the body by contacting objects, it is called "nutriment" (āhāra);
this is a designation based on its function.
Alternatively,
it may be that "contact" itself is designated as food based on its essential nature.
Third is the food of volition.
That which involves expectation is called volition (*cetanā*).
Because volition is able to nourish and develop [the mind], it is called nutriment (*āhāra*);
it is named according to its function.
Alternatively,
it may be that volition itself is the nutriment;
the name is applied to its essential nature.
The fourth is the nutriment of consciousness (*vijñānāhāra*). That which has the nature of discerning is called consciousness;
this consciousness itself is the nutriment.
It may be that the essence itself constitutes the name;
alternatively, it may be that the eighth consciousness, by virtue of its sustaining function, is called "food."
It is named according to its function.
Second, regarding the manifestation of its essence (*tattva*),
there are two ways of discerning that essence.
First, the Hīnayāna;
second, the Mahāyāna.

Within the Hīnayāna, schools such as the Sarvāstivāda and the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra* maintain that the substance of the fast consists of the three sense objects: fragrance, flavor, and tangibility.

Because these are known through internal cognition as the sustenance of their own faculties, the food of contact (*sparśāhāra*) and the food of volition (*manosaṃcetanāhāra*) take the two mental factors of contact and volition—both of which belong to the universal ground (*mahābhūmika*)—as their essence.
The food of consciousness (*vijñānāhāra*) takes the six consciousnesses, as the sovereign mind-kings, as its essence.
According to the Sautrāntika school and the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*, fasting consists of the four objective bases—visible form, odor, flavor, and tangibility—as its substance;
whereas eating consists of the conventional tangibility produced by conditions such as cold and heat as its substance.
The food of volition is characterized by seeking through volition; its essence is the mind of volition.
The food of consciousness takes as its essence the five sensory consciousnesses, the mental consciousness that follows them, and the independent mental consciousness.
In the Mahāyāna treatises such as the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fasting (*āhāra-pratiṣedha*) takes the three objects—odor, flavor, and tangibility—as its essence.

Food (*āhāra*), on the other hand, takes the factor of contact (*sparśa*) among the universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*) as its essence. Although contact is common to both the seventh and eighth consciousnesses, [it is specifically the contact associated with the sixth consciousness that constitutes food].
The meaning of "nutriment" (*āhāra*) is most prominent in its association with the six consciousnesses.
The nutriment of volition (*manosaṃcetanā-āhāra*) also takes the mental factor of volition (*cetanā*) from among the universal factors (*mahābhūmika*) as its essence.
Although this volition is associated with all the consciousnesses, [it is specifically designated as such].
Regarding those belonging to the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), the meaning of "nutriment" (*āhāra*) is predominant.

The nutriment of consciousness (*vijñānāhāra*) has the *ālayavijñāna* as its essence. Although this consciousness extends to the seventh and eighth [consciousnesses], it is [here] specifically the *ālayavijñāna*.
The eighth is the excellence of the meaning of food.
Regarding the third, the establishment [of the stages],
there are four dharmas according to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.
First, vigor; second, joy;
third, aspiration;
fourth, sustenance.
The sense faculties and the primary elements nourish the physical body through the food of abstention from eating,
because they possess vitality;
through the food of contact, they are sustained by joy and pleasure, thereby enabling the growth and maintenance of the sense faculties and the primary elements.
By means of the nutriment of volition (*manahsaṃcetanāhāra*), one focuses with longing so that the sense-faculties (*rūpindriya*) are nourished and maintained in continuity.
By means of the nutriment of consciousness (*vijñānāhāra*), one maintains the appropriation (*upādāna*) of the sense-faculties and the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) so that they do not cease.
The four types of nutriment are established based on these four meanings.
Fourth, regarding the analysis of their distinctions,
according to the *Anabhāvavāda-śāstra* (Treatise on Non-nature):
There are four kinds of nutriment.
First is the nutriment that sustains an impure basis;
this refers to ordinary beings of the desire realm who, because they possess afflictions, are said to have an impure basis.
The "present body" refers to the impure body.
Because it subsists by relying on these four kinds of nutriment, it is called "subsistence through nutriment based on the impure.
Second is "subsistence through nutriment based on both the pure and the impure."

This refers to noble learners (*śaikṣa*) and ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) of the form and formless realms. For noble learners, the view-delusions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) having been completely abandoned is termed "pure";
that the cultivation-delusions (*bhāvanā-kleśa*) have not yet been exhausted is termed "impure."
When ordinary beings have attained the higher meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) and have suppressed or severed the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the desire realm, they are termed "pure.
As long as they have not yet abandoned the afflictions of the higher realms, they are termed "impure.
Because these four nutriments (*āhāra*) sustain and maintain their existence, it is said that they "abide by means of food" as their pure or impure support.

The three types of pure reliance on sustenance (*āhāra*) refer to Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas who, having completely severed the afflictions of both the path of seeing and the path of cultivation, are termed "pure.
Because they are able to abide by means of these four kinds of sustenance, it is called "pure abiding in sustenance."
Fourth is the manifestation of dwelling by means of sustenance.
The Buddhas, Tathāgatas, and Bodhisattvas of great majesty do not rely on material food for sustenance, yet they manifest the acceptance of food so that their bodies may remain.
Regarding the term "Bodhisattva of Great Majestic Virtue" (Mahātejas):
it refers to those from the eighth stage upward who have realized effortless mastery and manifest sovereign majestic virtue; this interpretation is also acceptable.
From the first bhūmi upward, attaining the ten kinds of mastery is called "majestic power" (vaibhutva).
Alternatively,

it may refer to the majestic power and mastery over the transformation-body (nairmāṇika-kāya) attained by those of the two vehicles who have turned their minds toward the Mahāyāna and received the retribution of the transformation-death (pariṇāmika-maraṇa).
These bodhisattvas transform their bodies and minds such that they do not require the sustenance of food;
rather, they manifest emanation bodies (nirmāṇakāya) to demonstrate the act of eating.
This fragrant cake is precisely the fourth demonstration of reliance upon food.
Alternatively,
it may be that the nature of this dharma-food is untainted (anāsrava) and is therefore not subsumed under the four types of food, such as the food of physical nutriment and so forth.
Regarding the fifth point, the presence or absence [of sustenance] within the realms and destinies:
the desire realm possesses all four types of nutriment;
the form realm and the formless realm possess only three.
Because this fasting occurs only in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), if categorized according to the five destinies (*pañcagati*),
it can be understood as pertaining to humans and devas.
The three lower miserable realms also possess the four kinds of nutriment.
The *Yogācārabhūmi* states:
"Sentient beings in the hells also have subtle forms of fasting."
This refers to the subtle winds within the internal organs;
by virtue of these causes and conditions, they are able to endure for a long time.
This concludes the sixth question-and-answer analysis.
Question: Is it the case that all things which are consumed constitute food?
Answer: No.
One should formulate four propositions as appropriate.
There may be things that are cut but are not food;
that is to say, those things which cannot nourish the sense faculties (*indriya*) and the primary elements (*mahābhūta*).
There may be that which is nutriment but not a substance that is cut;
all other three nutriments are without form and are not cut.
There may also be that which is both nutriment and a substance that is cut.
That is to say, various fasts can cause the sense faculties (*indriya*) and the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) to be nourished;
however, there are also things that are neither fasts nor food—
namely, contact (*sparśa*), volition (*cetanā*), consciousness (*vijñāna*), and so forth— which cannot nourish the sense faculties and the primary elements.
In this manner, the remaining [factors] should each be treated as fourfold propositions according to their respective applications.
Question:
Do sleep, dreaming, celibacy, and meditative concentration all nourish the sense faculties and the primary elements?
Why is nutriment not established [as a separate category]? Answer:
There are two kinds of nourishment.
First is nourishment through the gathering of specific meanings,
which refers to nurturing the sense faculties so that they become clear and flourishing.
Second is nourishment by ensuring they are free from harm.
It is able to maintain the great elements of the sense faculties without impairment;
such nourishment exists in dreams and the like, whereas it is entirely absent in the aforementioned [waking] state.
Therefore, it is not established.
Question:
There are fifty-one kinds of phenomena subsumed under mental factors (*caitta*).
Why are contact (*sparśa*) and volition (*cetanā*) specifically designated as "nutriments" (*āhāra*), while the others are not so established?
Answer: Because contact benefits the body by means of its objects, and volition benefits the mind through aspiration.
Second, establishing that what remains after eating is not called "food.
Question:
Are these four kinds of food with outflows (sāsrava) or without outflows (anāsrava)?
Answer: It is exclusively with outflows (sāsrava).
The reason for this is as follows:
By means of these four nutriments, the body of existence is sustained;
because the untainted dharmas (*anāsrava-dharma*) can destroy the body of existence, they are not called "nutriments.
If one follows the Mahāyāna perspective:
Because it is sustained by the joy and bliss of the flavor of the Dharma, even untainted dharmas (*anāsrava-dharma*) can support and nourish the life-force of wisdom;
thus they are also called "food.
The fragrant rice of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) is likewise the same as this.
Question:
Among the three natures, under which nature are the four nutriments, such as "cutting off" and so forth, subsumed? Answer:
The two nutriments of consciousness and contact are exclusively indeterminate (avyākṛta) by nature;
the two nutriments of volition and contact logically pertain to all three natures.
Question:
Fasting has a physical form that can be manifested;
as for the other three, which are mental, how can they be manifested? Answer:
The mind can also manifest.
As stated in the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*,
the transformation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) of the Buddhas possess minds that depend on others, but lack minds that depend on themselves.
That which relies on the minds of others refers to the mind of transformation through signs (*nirmāṇa-nimitta-citta*).
Furthermore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"Transform immeasurable sentient beings and cause them to possess a mind."
Therefore, one knows that the mind can also manifest;
this is truly because the inconceivable meditative concentrations (*samādhi*) of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are able to conjure forth phenomena that lack physical form or substance.
If the Buddhas did not manifest transformation-minds (*nirmāṇa-citta*),
how could those of the two vehicles, ordinary beings, animals, and others know the Buddha’s mind?
Even Bodhisattvas of the ten stages cannot know the World-Honored One’s true mind.
Regarding "gardens, groves, terraces, and towers":
it refers to entering the stages of sagehood by beholding these terraces and towers.
Regarding the "thirty-two marks": one may see one mark, two marks, or even many marks.
He manifests according to what is appropriate for each being;
all these are conditions for entering the Way.
By "the Buddha-body," he means the manifestation of the Golden Body (kāya).
There are sentient beings who, upon seeing the Buddha’s form-body, resolve their minds and awaken to the Way.
These three preceding phrases indicate that the visual consciousness can serve as the gateway for the sensory object of form to function as a Buddha-work.
As for the "Buddha-work of empty space":
By removing forms and appearances, one manifests the sign of empty space, causing the mind to become tranquil;
thus, karmic entanglements naturally dissipate.
This is just as Mañjuśrī manifested the sign of empty space by extinguishing all material forms in order to transform King Ajātaśatru.
Therefore, awakening to this path means that the consciousness passing through the sense-object of dharmas constitutes a Buddha-work.
Below, it is explained how sentient beings should, by means of these conditions, attain entry into the practice of the Vinaya.
Although the causes of their practice differ, they both enter into the conduct of the Vinaya.
Furthermore, those who rely on metaphors such as dreams and illusions understand the Dharma and thereby attain enlightenment;
likewise, those who rely on sounds and language [attain it].
Nowadays, one attains the Way through verbal teachings.
These two preceding lines show that the ear-consciousness can serve as the medium for the sound-dust to perform Buddha-work.
As for "silence and wordlessness":
This is precisely the same category as Vimalakīrti’s silence; it is the faculty of mental consciousness that can serve as a medium for the sensory objects of the Dharma to perform Buddha-work.
Thus, Ānanda, such are the majestic deportments of all Buddhas.
This sentence generally reveals that the Dharmakāya, through its non-conceptual realization, accords with the capacities of sentient beings so that there is nothing that does not benefit them.
"Dignified deportment" refers to the four physical modes of conduct: walking, standing, sitting, and reclining.
Regarding "advancing and halting":
lifting, moving, looking up, and looking down are called advancing;
staying still and lying down are called halting.
All that is performed— whether through seeing,
hearing, sensing, or cognizing— is the activity of the three karmas.
Since there has never been anything therein that is without benefit, it is said that nothing is not the work of the Buddha.
This means that the six consciousnesses are able to serve as the conduit for the six sense objects to perform the Buddha-work.
The fourteen preceding phrases describe the performance of Buddha-work in accordance with the flow [of phenomena].
Furthermore, regarding these four māras:
The line following "eighty-four thousand afflictions" concerns the Buddha-work of逆行 (pratiloma).
Regarding the "gates of the eighty-four thousand afflictions":
As stated in the *Sutra of the Wise and the Foolish*,
there was a bodhisattva named King Joy who thought to himself:
"What samādhi must one practice to swiftly attain the eighty-four thousand dharma-gates of the pāramitās?
Having reflected thus, he requested this of the Buddha,
and the Buddha then replied to him, saying:
There is a samādhi named "Comprehending the Root of All Dharmas.
When a bodhisattva practices it, they swiftly attain eighty-four thousand dharma-gates of the various pāramitās. What are these?
That Buddha answered in full detail;
from the stage of the Infinite Radiance (Apramāṇābhā) up to the stage of Distributing Relics (Śarīrapratiṣṭhāpana), there are three hundred and fifty kinds of gates,
each of which cultivates the causes of the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā).
There are thus two thousand one hundred pāramitās; by means of these pāramitās,
one counteracts the afflictions of the four great elements and the six decays,
resulting in twenty-one thousand pāramitās.
It is precisely because ordinary beings take those four great elements as their body,
whereas the noble ones, by practicing the various perfections, attain the pure Dharma-body;
thus, abandoning those four great elements is called "antidote."
The six decays (*ṣaḍāyatana*) are great thieves, namely the six objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*),
because they can cause all wholesome dharmas to decline and waste away.
Through the noble cultivation of the various perfections (*pāramitā*), one realizes entry into the realm of the Buddha.
Abandoning those six sense objects is called "curing the six decays.
Employing these twenty-one thousand perfections to cure the four mental illnesses—
namely, greed, hatred, delusion, and their equal combination— is the practice.
Each of these four categories contains twenty-one thousand [afflictions],
totaling eighty-four thousand afflictions;
yet sentient beings are wearied by them.
Ordinary, foolish sentient beings, because they arrive [at existence] through delusion, regard it as a gate of exhaustion;
the Buddhas, however, realize that the nature of afflictions is empty,
and thus use the emptiness of afflictions to teach and transform sentient beings.
Therefore, attaining awakening is called "Buddha-work.
Thus, the Vimalakīrti Sūtra states:
"All Tathāgatas perform Buddha-work for all sentient beings precisely by means of this Dharma."
Therefore, the preceding sutra states:
"Afflictions are the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa),
because one knows them as they truly are."
Furthermore, the *Renwang jing* (Benevolent Kings Sūtra) states:
"As long as sentient beings have not yet attained Buddhahood,
bodhi is [regarded as] affliction (*kleśa*)."
If sentient beings were perfected,
the afflictions of a Buddha would become bodhi;
this is just as there are three grades among worldly physicians.
The inferior class of physicians treats what is not medicine as medicine;
those of middle quality treat medicine as medicine;
the superior class of skilled physicians treat what is not medicine as medicine.
The Buddha is also like this:
being able to transform all afflictions entirely into nirvana is what is called the work of a Buddha.
Yuan says: "The afflictions of all Buddhas have already been abandoned;
subsequently, great compassion manifests within the wisdom attained after [meditative equipoise] to gather and transform sentient beings."
Sentient beings attain awakening by means of this;
thus it is called "Buddha-work.
It is precisely because this mental consciousness can serve as a conduit for the dharmas of the sense-field that it constitutes Buddha-work.
The third section below summarizes.
From here on, the third part clarifies the equality of all phenomena.
Within this text, there are three sections.
First, it clarifies the equality of the Bodhisattvas' minds;
second, it clarifies the equality of the Buddhas' virtues;
third, it reveals the superiority [of the Mahāyāna] by contrasting the scriptural authority (*śāstra-pramāṇa*) of the Great and Small Vehicles.
Regarding those bodhisattvas who previously entered this gate:
it refers to bodhisattvas who have attained *kṣānti* (receptivity) and have realized entry into the gate of the equal Dharma of all Buddhas.
If they see any pure and wondrous buddha-fields, they do not regard them with joy.
Regarding "not being covetous or arrogant":
upon first seeing [the Buddha], one does not rejoice; when reborn there, one is not covetous and remains unarrogant.
"Not regarding it as a cause for sorrow;
not being obstructed and not sinking" means that upon first seeing the impure land, one does not feel sorrow.
Rebirth is unimpeded;
dwelling therein, one does not sink.
Once the Bodhisattva has entered this gate, they know that the Buddha-body and the pure land are equal.
He is named "One Who Gives Rise to a Pure Mind," manifesting ten thousand differences to benefit all classes of beings;
therefore it is said that he is joyful, reverent, and unprecedented.
This is none other than the Bodhisattva Vyūharāja-gandha.
In the second section, which clarifies the equality of the Buddha’s virtues,
the first part clarifies the equality of essence.

Regarding the subsequent sections such as "the name" and so forth: in the preceding middle section, there is first the *dharma* (the principle), next the *udāharaṇa* (the example), and finally the *upanaya* (the application).
Within the *dharma*, there are two parts.
The first section clarifies that the self-attained virtues of all Buddhas are equal;
following the phrase "for the sake of transforming [sentient beings]," the subsequent section clarifies that the manifestations of the Buddhas' transformative activities differ.
Within the analogy, there are likewise two parts.
The various examples given for the earth illustrate the preceding second section on the conditions for transforming sentient beings.
That space has no such variety illustrates the aforementioned equality of one's own virtuous nature.
Within the application [of the analogy],
there are two parts. The first consists of two sentences,
which individually apply the preceding analogy.
Ānanda, regarding the physical bodies (*rūpakāya*) of all Buddhas, the following provides a general synthesis of the preceding metaphors.
In the previous section on individual synthesis, they were matched in sequential order;
the meaning of both may be understood accordingly.
Within the synthesis, one does not differentiate between the two kinds of supreme qualities— those of oneself and those of others—
as they are all equally empty above; therefore, it is called "synthesis."
Regarding the form-bodies (*rūpakāya*) of all Buddhas:
they are equal as a single form-body;
the untainted aggregates of form (*anāsravarūpaskandha*) are entirely equal.
Second, regarding majesty and so forth:
this is because the form-body (*rūpakāya*) possesses supreme majestic virtue. Third, regarding the marks (*lakṣaṇa*) and so forth.
Because of their thirty-two marks,
their fourfold natures, and so forth,
their spiritual dispositions differ.
There are two kinds:
first, the cultivated seed;
second, the innate seed.
Regarding the "nature of practice" (*śikṣāgotra*): it is called the nature of practice because it is obtained through the perfuming of hearing [the Dharma].
An ancient commentary states:
"That which is called *tathatā* (suchness) or Buddha-nature exists inherently by its very nature."
If it is explained as it is here,
this refers to the inherent functional capacity of the seeds that exist by the very nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*),
namely, the "active" Buddha-nature (*pravṛtti-buddhadhātu*).
Therefore, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states:
"From beginningless time, the six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana) have been a distinct excellence, continuing in succession;
that which is obtained through the very nature of phenomena (dharmatā) constitutes its essence."
Alternatively, it may be so.
"Gotra" (lineage) refers to one's clan.
Thus, the Vimalakīrtinirdeśa Sūtra says:
"Lineage" refers to noble birth.
The five precepts, meditative concentration,
and so forth constitute the equality of the fivefold merits.
The six [perfections] and thirty-two virtues are equal,
namely, the possession of the powers, the fearlessnesses, and the unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*).
Great compassion is the virtue that benefits others below.
The mental action of compassion;
the bodily action of dignified deportment;
and the vocal action of preaching the Dharma, and so forth.
"To bring sentient beings to maturity" means to benefit those of the three vehicles.
"To purify the Buddha-lands" means...
The immeasurable pure land.
That which possesses all Buddha-dharmas refers to the Buddha-dharmas of the three bodies.

"Samyaksaṃbuddha" is first of all a praise of the title "Perfectly All-Knowing.

"Tathāgata" is a title of praise for the Tathāgata.

"The Tathāgata comes from nowhere and goes nowhere; therefore he is called the Tathāgata.
*Buddha* is a title praising Great Enlightenment.

In purity, one does not take delight in purity;

When practicing the path,

As one traverses suffering, one should be ever more diligent;
even when beset by the threats of Māra and his enmity, the mind should not give rise to weariness. This may be so.
When a bodhisattva teaches and transforms sentient beings, they do not mix their practice with craving or views.

because they are free from views, they do so without fatigue.
Regarding those who practice the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) instantaneously:
for those within the realm of sentient beings who have not yet resolved their minds [toward awakening], they employ generosity and kind speech to gather them and cause them to resolve their minds;

Those who have already practiced employ the means of "acting in concert" (*samānārthatā*) to bring others to liberation.
Because Bodhisattvas focus their minds on practicing the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), it is called "conforming practice.
To protect the Dharma without sparing even one's own body or life—this is [the meaning].

seeking with a non-regressive mind is called "abiding in skill.

This is because a bodhisattva manifests in the form of a Brahmā king to exhort the Buddha to preach the Dharma, and thereby obtains the retribution of the Buddha’s voice.
It is further said:
Because one sees the various wholesome deeds performed by sentient beings and rejoices in them with praise, one obtains the retribution of the Buddha’s eightfold voice.
As for these eight tones:
First, subtle;
second, supple; third, harmonious and appropriate.
Fourth, thorough understanding of the Four Truths;
fifth, not being female;
sixth, not being mistaken.
Seventh, profound;
eighth, inexhaustible.
Regarding the excellence of body, speech, and mind, one attains the majestic deportment of a Buddha.
The goodness of the three karmas attains the majestic deportment of a Buddha;
these superior retributions— the four modes of deportment of a Buddha—
are all considered Buddha-activities.
Although the Bodhisattva has not yet fully perfected all the factors,
it is said that they "have attained" them because they have entered its sphere.
It is also said:
That one's deportment is similar to that of a Buddha is also called "attainment.
That one who deeply cultivates wholesome dharmas becomes increasingly superior in their practice clarifies the inclusion of the bodhisattva’s virtues.
Practicing reasonability oneself is called "profound cultivation";
the gradual increase in benefiting others is called "progressively superior practice.
Those who establish the bodhisattva-saṃgha through the Mahāyāna teachings [are thus described].
Based on the Mahāyāna teachings, one initiates practice and becomes a member of the Bodhisattva Saṃgha.
There are two kinds of Bodhisattva Saṃgha:
first, those who are householders and possess only concord in principle (*dharmasāmagrī*).
The two types— the renunciant and the householder—
and the two harmonies (of body and mind) are both subsumed within the Bodhisattva Saṃgha.
For Śrāvakas, however, one must necessarily possess both the renunciant and householder aspects, as well as the two harmonies, to be designated as a Saṃgha.
Those who live at home are not the Saṃgha.
Those whose minds are free from negligence and do not lose their manifold virtues are the ones who have overcome greed.
The five desires are called heedlessness;
alternatively,
grasping at signs and conceptual discrimination are called heedlessness.
Due to negligence, one loses all wholesome qualities;
when the mind is free from negligence, there is no wholesome quality that is not accumulated.
Among these three statements, the first is the most excellent practice.
The second is the excellence of the dharma;
the third is the excellence of the mind.
Thus far, the practice has been extensively analyzed in this manner.
The following serves as a general conclusion.
What follows constitutes the second section, which explains the aforementioned non-abiding in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
This section contains three parts.
First, the restatement;
second, the explanation;
last, the conclusion.
Regarding the statement that "a bodhisattva does not abide in the unconditioned":
while those of the two vehicles contemplate the unconditioned and abide in the bliss of the unconditioned,

how is it that a bodhisattva, though contemplating the bliss of the unconditioned, is able to refrain from realizing it and instead remains forever within birth and death to teach and transform sentient beings?
The explanation is divided into three parts.
The first part consists of three phrases, which constitute the three gateways of the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
Next are four lines concerning the four gates of Dharma-practice.
Below are eight lines.
Regarding the "Successive Dharma-Gate of Contemplation":
as for the statement that one practices emptiness but does not take emptiness as a realization,
Manzhu said:
The Bodhisattva’s thorough understanding that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature is called the cultivation of emptiness.
Since emptiness itself is also empty,
he does not realize it [as a final state].
A proverb says:
"By the power of wisdom, one contemplates emptiness;
by the power of compassion, one does not realize [nirvana] prematurely."
Hongfu said: "Emptiness is of two kinds:
first, the emptiness of that which is known."
This refers to the emptiness of persons and phenomena;
second, the emptiness of the wisdom that contemplates;
and the emptiness of the wisdom that contemplates the object of contemplation is called the emptiness of cultivation and study.
The wisdom of contemplation is also empty;
this is called not taking emptiness as a realization.
One cultivates signlessness and wishlessness.
Regarding "not taking non-action and signlessness as realization," Man states:
"Because it is empty, it is signless."
That which cannot be produced by causes is called "non-action" (wu-jo).
Since neither marks nor non-action can be apprehended, there is no realization.
As the proverb says:
Because of the observation of wisdom, there is signlessness and non-action;
because of the power of compassion, one does not grasp at signs and thus does not realize [nirvana]. Hongfu says:
There are two kinds of signlessness:
first, the signlessness of the knowable,
which refers to the principle of the two kinds of selflessness.
Second is the wisdom of the signless contemplation:
the wisdom that contemplates the two kinds of selflessness, perceiving neither the mark of a person nor the mark of phenomena,
is called the training in the wisdom of signless contemplation.
"Signlessness" (animitta) does not mean taking signlessness as a realization.
Regarding the phrase "cultivating non-arising through non-realization," Sengzhao says:
All phenomena exist through the convergence of conditions and cease when conditions disperse.
What phenomenon could there be that exists prior to depending on conditions for its arising?
This is another name for the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*); there is no fruit that can arise.
Since the nature of non-arising is empty, and non-arising itself is not "non-arising," it is said that one does not take non-arising as a proof.
It is further stated:
"There are two kinds of non-arising:
first, the non-arising of the knowable."
That is to say: first, contemplating that the dharmas of causes and conditions have no abiding;
second, contemplating that wisdom has no arising.
Regarding these two absences of self, first contemplating the emptiness of the nature of causes and conditions is called "cultivating non-arising."
The wisdom of contemplation is also empty; this does not mean that one takes the non-arising of phenomena as proof.
Regarding the contemplation of impermanence, the following clarifies the Mahāyāna contemplation of the four seals of equality.
As for "contemplating impermanence without wearying of the roots of goodness":
Manzhi said:
"The followers of the Two Vehicles regard impermanence as impermanent and thus feel aversion toward conditioned wholesome dharmas;
Bodhisattvas, however, do not regard impermanence as impermanent, for they know that the nature of impermanence is empty."
However, because his merit is not yet complete, he is able to never tire of the roots of goodness. Hongfu says:
"Observing impermanence allows one to leave behind the inversion of permanence, yet not tiring of the roots of goodness reveals the fundamental nature of permanence."
It is further said:
Because of great wisdom, having seen that the five aggregates are impermanent, one is already free from the inversion of permanence;
because of great compassion, one remains constantly within birth and death to teach and transform sentient beings, planting all manner of roots of goodness.
Regarding the statement, "One who contemplates the suffering of the world does not loathe birth and death," Faman says:
Because those of the Two Vehicles regard suffering as suffering, they loathe birth and death.
The Great Being knows that suffering is unborn, yet he dwells within suffering to transform sentient beings; therefore, he does not loathe birth and death.
Thus, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says:
"It is not that the Bodhisattva is without suffering."
Because one understands suffering, there is no suffering.
The *Sāṃkathyaviniścaya-sūtra* states:
"To know that suffering is without arising is called the Noble Truth of Suffering."
Based on this textual evidence, we know that a bodhisattva must fully realize that suffering is not [inherently] suffering before they can abide in the middle way to transform sentient beings.
Hongfu says: "Observing the suffering of the three realms, one attains detachment from the inversion of regarding pleasure as [true] happiness, yet does not loathe birth and death."
There is also the contemplation of the nature of happiness within birth and death.
Regarding the one who does not grow weary of repenting for their lack of self, Pūrṇa said:
Because the followers of the Hīnayāna regard non-self as non-self, they are negligent in admonishing others.
The Mahāsattva knows that both the dharmas of self and non-self are empty;
yet sentient beings have not yet realized this.
Therefore, one repents without weariness. Hongfu said:
"To contemplate non-self."
Observing that arising is selfless, one is forever free from the inversion of regarding it as a self;
yet, never wearying in exhorting others,
one constantly encourages and transforms sentient beings to lead them to realize the true self.
This is what is called Buddha-nature.
Regarding the observation of quiescence as "eternal extinction," Faman says:
The śrāvakas regard quiescence as being quiescent;
therefore, they realize extinction.
The Mahāsattva, however, contemplates that all phenomena are originally quiescent and extinguished, rather than becoming extinguished for the first time now.
For this reason, they do not realize [nirvana].
Thus, the aforementioned sutra says:
"The Dharma is fundamentally not so."
"Now, there is no cessation;
this is the meaning of *śānti* (quiescence). Hongfu said.
Regarding those who contemplate quiescence:
although they know that nirvāṇa is unconditioned, eternal, and blissful,
they do not enter extinction because they abide in great compassion to transform sentient beings.
From this point downward, there are eight phrases that clarify contemplation through the sequence of dharmas.
Regarding "contemplating detachment while cultivating goodness with body and mind":
contemplating the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) as being free from the characteristics of body and mind is called the contemplation of detachment.
In order to fulfill virtuous conduct and achieve enlightenment,
it may be appropriate to cultivate goodness through both body and mind.
There are three ways in which a bodhisattva is far removed from suffering:
first, being far removed from the fruit of suffering;
second, being far removed from afflictions.
Third, the lacquer of abandoning karma:
this refers to the state where emptiness is ever-present yet one does not practice and cultivate the good;
it is the observation that there is no destination for those who do not practice wholesome dharmas.
Sengzhao said:
"All phenomena have nowhere from which they come in the beginning and nowhere to which they return in the end.
Although one knows there is no place of return, one should always return to wholesome dharmas."
Alternatively,
by contemplating the true suchness of the two emptinesses,
one realizes that what arises is without anything arising.
Cessation has nothing that is ceased.
That which is neither born nor ceasing has no point of return.
Cultivating the patience of conformity (anulomikī-kṣānti) and returning toward the higher stages is called "attaining the excellence of non-arising."
Regarding those who contemplate non-arising yet bear the burden of all phenomena through the dharma of arising:
there are three ways in which a bodhisattva contemplates non-arising.
First, one contemplates that the intrinsic nature of the parikalpita (imagined) is non-arising.
Second, one contemplates that the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) does not arise from causes and conditions.
Third, one contemplates that the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) arises yet has nothing that truly arises.
Although one knows that all phenomena are without arising, for the sake of sentient beings one dwells within arising; thus, manifesting birth and preaching the Dharma, one delivers all beings.
Therefore, the preceding sutra says:
"Although one knows that there is neither arising nor ceasing,
for the sake of instructing others, one manifests birth."
Regarding "contemplating the outflow-free while not severing the various outflows":

from the first stage (*bhūmi*) up through the seventh stage, Bodhisattvas of sudden enlightenment simultaneously sever the two attachments to a personal self and to phenomena (*pudgala-dharma-grāha*), and realize the principle of *tathatā* (suchness); this is termed "contemplating the outflow-free."
Because they retain the seeds of innate greed to assist their vows for rebirth in order to bring benefit to sentient beings, it is said that "they do not sever the outflows (*āsrava*).
Alternatively,
it may be understood that Bodhisattvas from the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) upward, having realized the principle of the two-fold emptiness, are called "those who observe the outflow-free" (*anāsrava*).
The seeds of greed and so forth remaining are called "uninterrupted outflows" (*āsrava*).
Alternatively,
it may be said that they are called "uninterrupted outflows" because Bodhisattvas manifest within the realms of sentient beings characterized by outflows in order to transform them.
Regarding "observing that there is nothing to be practiced, yet using the practice of the Dharma to transform and give birth [to beings]," Zhaò says:
"The nature of dharmas (dharmatā) is without karma."
What is the practice?
Although one knows that there is no practice, sentient beings have not yet attained this realization;
therefore, one must cultivate sublime practices to transform and teach sentient beings.
Regarding "observing emptiness without abandoning great compassion":
one observes that the nature of phenomena is empty,
and that even emptiness is itself empty.
Sentient beings do not realize this;
therefore, he harbors compassion and does not abandon them.
He contemplates the state of correctness and does not follow the Lesser Vehicle.
The stage of the True Dharma is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Contemplating the emptiness of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is called the stage of the True Dharma;
therein, one does not cling to emptiness.
This is not like the realization attained by those of the Lesser Vehicle.
One contemplates that all phenomena are illusory, lacking solidity, devoid of a person, devoid of a master, and without marks; yet they are not without merit and wisdom.
All dharmas are produced through causes and conditions and possess no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
What constitutes its prison?
What constitutes its master?
Although they know this to be so, their great vows remain unfulfilled.
"How could one fail to cultivate merit and kindness simply because there is no host?
These various phrases all accomplish the non-abiding in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
This concludes the section on cultivating such dharmas.
Furthermore, following "endowed with merit," there are four pairs below.
These explain the aforementioned "neither exhausted nor abiding.
Why are these four pairs distinct?
First, the pair of merit and wisdom;
second, the pair of compassion and vow;
third, the pair of teaching and practice.
Regarding the four pairs of obstacles and their remedies:
these four pairs reduce to two ways of overcoming illness,
namely, the exhaustion of existence and the abiding in non-existence.
If one dwells in non-existence, both body and wisdom are lost;
how then can merit and wisdom be perfected?
To exhaust existence is precisely the cessation of contemplation.
If one abandons conditions, that is concentration;
it is possible to possess [concentration] even without compassion and vows. This may also be so.
The first [perfection] corresponds to one's own practice;
the latter three correspond to benefiting others.
Furthermore, "possessing merit and not abiding in the unconditioned" refers to this.
Now, the accumulation of virtue must necessarily involve crossing over the ford of existence;
if one dwells in non-action,
merit and virtue will not be complete.
Regarding the statement "one does not exhaust the conditioned through wisdom":
the clarity of wisdom must necessarily arise from vastness.
If one were to abandon the conditioned, [wisdom could not be realized].
Thus, their wisdom would not be complete.
As for "because of great compassion, they do not abide in the unconditioned":
how could one who enters birth through compassion be capable of abiding in non-existence?
Regarding "fulfilling one's original vows without exhausting the conditioned":
since vows arise from the accumulation of merit,
how could they be achieved by abandoning the conditioned?
Regarding "because they gather the medicine of the Dharma, they do not abide in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*"):
To gather excellent medicine, one must necessarily go to perilous mountains; it does not emerge from a flower hall.
When a Great Being gathers the medicine of the Dharma, it must necessarily be from the perils of existence; it is not produced within the unconditioned.
Regarding "following along with the reception of medicine, one does not exhaust the conditioned":
if one were to abandon the conditioned, one would be cut off from all living beings;
how then could one follow them and receive their medicine?
"Because he knows the illnesses of sentient beings, he does not abide in the unconditioned. This means that if one knows the origins of the various illnesses of sentient beings,
it is not something that can be accomplished by abiding in the unconditioned.
Regarding "not exhausting the conditioned in order to extinguish the illnesses of sentient beings":
to extinguish the illnesses of sentient beings, one must necessarily apply the remedy of existence;
how could this be accomplished by exhausting the conditioned?
From here below is the third section, which restates the conclusion and exhorts the study for all noble beings (*satpuruṣa*).
"The Bodhisattva has already cultivated this Dharma" refers back to the preceding two gates;
although these two dharmas differ, their practice is necessarily interdependent.
Therefore, I respond to and clarify this:
it is evident that practice and action each have their own distinct character, because the application of their functions differs.
This is called the final exhortation to practice and study.
Because one does not exhaust the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), there is no burden of lacking virtues;
because one does not dwell in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), there is no obstacle of solitary excellence.
These two gates of non-obstruction are the essential path for Bodhisattvas to propagate the Way and the source from which their manifold Buddha-activities proceed.

By exhorting others to study and demonstrating to them the inconceivable path of Buddha-activity so that they may examine it with certainty, one realizes that there are no distinctions among the Buddhas. Below, it clarifies how the Bodhisattva, having heard the Dharma, rejoices, pays homage, and takes his leave.
Within this, first there is the respectful service through the three types of action,
followed by the departure to return to their own lands.
Regarding the former, it is said at the outset that those bodhisattvas were all filled with joy upon hearing the teaching.
One makes an offering through the mental action of joy in the Dharma;
one makes an offering through the physical action of various flowers and so forth.
Among these, one first offers incense, flowers, and the like.
Thereafter, to establish reverence:
in the preceding section on making offerings, one scatters various exquisite flowers throughout the three thousandfold world-system as an offering to the Buddha Jewel;
furthermore, this sutra speaks of making offerings to the Dharma Jewel.
Together with all the bodhisattvas, they made offerings to the Jewel of the Saṃgha.
Having completed the offerings above,
the following section sets forth their expressions of reverence.
This concludes the section on bodily action (*kāyakarman*).
The passage beginning with "Praising what has never been before" (*āścaryādbhutadharma*) concerns the praise that constitutes verbal action (*vākkarman*) as an offering.
Thus, the preceding section on reverent offerings is concluded.
Having spoken thus, he disappeared and returned to his own land.

there are two kinds of vision.

Within the true reality of all phenomena,

there is neither arising nor ceasing.
Quiescent and extinguished like nirvāṇa.
There are three ways of contemplating the Buddha:
first, contemplating the nirmāṇakāya (emanation body).

which is the true suchness (tathatā) of the two emptinesses.
